The Encyclopedia of the Path

Every word this library uses, defined plainly. Type any spelling you have seen, in any transliteration, and the meaning arrives with its evidence beside it. 523 words, and it grows whenever a reader tells us one was missing.

523 words

#

Pardon: dropping a wrong you are owed, without the other person having to earn it.

The Qur'an asks whether you would not love Allah to forgive you, in the middle of telling a wronged man to pardon (Qur'an 24:22), and says the reward of the one who pardons and reconciles is with Allah (Qur'an 42:40). Scholars distinguish 'afw, letting the debt go, from safh, letting the resentment go with it. The Prophet peace be upon him said Allah only increases a servant in honour for pardoning, in Muslim.

also written Afw · Afu · Afuw · Al-Afuww · Safh · Pardon

see also

A contract: a binding agreement formed by an offer and its acceptance.

The word means a knot or a tie, and Surah al-Ma'idah opens by telling believers to fulfil their contracts. Fiqh requires clear terms, a lawful subject matter, and consent free of coercion and deception. The Hanbali rule is the most generous of the four, holding any contract valid unless a text forbids it, which leaves wide room for new commercial forms, and modern Islamic finance leans on that opening.

also written Aqd · Aqad · Akd · Uqud · Aqood · Aqd nikah

see also

The part of the body that must be covered, which varies by person and by setting.

For a man all four schools say from the navel to the knee. For a woman before unrelated men the schools differ: the majority cover everything except the face and hands, some Hanbalis and later Shafi'is include the face, and Hanafis also exempt the feet. Among other women and before mahrams the requirement is much lighter, and in prayer it differs again. It is a rule about dignity in company, not a claim that the body is shameful.

also written Awrah · Aurah · Awra · Aura · Awrat · Aurat

see also

The evil eye: real harm that can follow an admiring or an envious look.

The Prophet peace be upon him said the eye is true, in Bukhari and Muslim, and in a report in Malik's Muwatta he instructed a man whose look had harmed another to wash, and the water was poured over the one affected. It can come from someone who wishes you no harm at all, which is why the Sunnah answer is to ask Allah to bless what you admire. Treatment is ruqya and the prophetic supplications. It is not a reason to hide your life or to start suspecting your neighbours.

also written Ayn · Al-ayn · Ain · Ayin · Ayn hasid · Nazar

see also

The original ruling, before any concession applies: the default rather than the exception.

'Azimah and rukhsah are a matched pair. Praying four rak'ahs is the 'azimah; shortening them on a journey is the rukhsah. Scholars differ over which is better for someone who qualifies for a concession, though most hold that where the Prophet clearly took the concession himself, as with breaking the fast on a hard journey, taking it is preferred.

also written Azimah · Azima · Azeemah · Azimat · Aziymah · the original ruling

see also

The waiting period a woman observes after divorce or a husband's death before remarrying.

After divorce it is three quru', which Hanafis and Hanbalis read as menstrual cycles and Malikis and Shafi'is as the purities between them, or three months for a woman who does not menstruate; after a husband's death, four months and ten days; and if she is pregnant, until she gives birth. Its purposes are to show there is no pregnancy, to leave room for reconciliation, and to mark the ending. In a revocable divorce she keeps housing and maintenance, and the husband may take her back without a new contract.

also written Iddah · Idda · Iddat · Eddah · Iddah period · Idat

see also

Self-admiration: being impressed by your own good deed as though you produced it alone.

The Qur'an tells people not to claim purity for themselves (Qur'an 53:32). Scholars distinguish it from kibr: kibr needs someone to look down on, while 'ujb only needs a mirror. It is treated by remembering that the ability, the opportunity and the guidance were all given, and by noticing how quickly a deed you are proud of stops feeling sincere.

also written Ujb · Ujub · Ajab · Ghurur · Self-admiration · Vanity

see also

Local custom, which fiqh accepts as a decider where revelation has left a matter open.

If a contract says a reasonable quantity, or a delivery in good time, it is 'urf that decides what those words mean. It cannot make lawful what the texts forbid; it fills gaps and defines undefined terms. Because customs change, rulings resting on 'urf change with them, which is why the same school can give different answers in different centuries or countries without contradicting itself.

also written Urf · Orf · Urff · Aadah · Adah · Ada

see also

A

The Prophet's closest friend, his companion in the cave, and the first caliph.

He is called as-Siddiq, the one who confirms, for believing the night journey without hesitation when others scoffed. He freed Bilal and other tortured slaves with his own money, and the Prophet appointed him to lead the prayer in his final illness. His caliphate lasted about two years and was mostly spent holding the community together through the wars of apostasy; he also ordered the Qur'an gathered into a single written copy. He is buried beside the Prophet.

also written Abu Bakr as-Siddiq · Abubakar · Abu Bakar · Abu Bakr Siddique · Ebubekir · Abubakr

see also

The Companion who narrated more hadith than any other, from about four years in the Prophet's company.

The nickname means father of the kitten, from a cat he carried as a boy. He accepted Islam around the year of Khaybar, joined the poor Companions living on the mosque bench, and stayed close to the Prophet while others worked or traded. He said openly that the Muhajirun were busy in the markets and the Ansar with their land, and he was not. He also asked the Prophet to pray that he would not forget, and reported that he never forgot anything afterwards.

also written Abu Hurairah · Abu Huraira · Abu Hurayra · Abu Hureyre · Ebu Hureyre · Abdur Rahman ibn Sakhr

see also

Good manner in a specific situation: the right way to sit, speak, eat, enter, and ask.

Where akhlaq names the character underneath, adab names the outward form it takes here and now, and most of it was taught by example. Classical scholars wrote whole books on it, such as al-Bukhari's al-Adab al-Mufrad. Some adab is fixed by the Sunnah, such as eating with the right hand, and some varies with place and custom, which is why a practice can be good manners in one country and odd in another.

also written Adaab · Aadab · Aadaab · Adab al-mufrad · Etiquette · Manners

see also

The uprightness of a narrator: sane, adult, Muslim, not openly sinful, not known for shameful habits.

Adalah is about character, not perfection. A narrator does not need to be a saint, but he must not be known for lying, for open sin, or for behaviour suggesting he does not care what people think of him. It is one half of being thiqah. The other half is dabt.

also written Adala · Adaalah · Adalat · Adaalat · Adl · Aadalah

see also

The punishment or ease a person meets in the grave, before the Day of Judgement arrives.

The Qur'an describes the people of Fir'awn exposed to the Fire morning and evening before the Hour comes (Qur'an 40:46), and many sound hadiths describe the grave as either a garden of Paradise or a pit of the Fire. Ahl al-Sunnah affirm it as real without claiming to know how it works upon a body that has decayed or was never buried. The Mu'tazila denied it; the Sunni schools do not.

also written Azab al-Qabr · Adhab ul Qabr · Azab e Qabr · Qabr azab · Punishment of the grave · Torment of the grave

see also

The call announcing that a prayer time has entered, given aloud before each obligatory prayer.

It was taught to the companions in Madinah after they discussed how to gather people, and Bilal was its first caller. Its lines declare Allah's greatness, the testimony of faith, and the summons to prayer and to success. The Fajr adhan adds the line that prayer is better than sleep. The one who calls it is the muezzin.

also written Azan · Athan · Adan · Ezan · Azaan · Adhaan

see also

The set remembrances of the day: morning, evening, sleeping, waking, eating, travel and distress.

These are supplications the Prophet peace be upon him taught for particular moments, gathered in works such as al-Nawawi's al-Adhkar and, in our time, Hisn al-Muslim. Attaching remembrance to fixed times rather than to feelings is what allows it to survive a bad week. The wording is best kept as it was narrated, and the strength of the reports varies, so reliable collections mark which ones are authentic.

also written Azkar · Adhkaar · Azkaar · Adkar · Morning adhkar · Evening adhkar

see also

Any hadith that does not reach the level of mutawatir, however strong its single chain may be.

Most hadiths, including most of the two Sahihs, are ahad. Scholars agree that an authentic ahad report is acted upon in law. They differ about creed: hadith scholars and the Hanbalis generally accept authentic ahad reports in matters of belief, while many Ash'ari, Maturidi and Hanafi theologians held that such reports give strong probability rather than certainty, and so accepted them without building charges of unbelief on them.

also written Aahad · Ahaad · Khabar al-wahid · Khabar wahid · Khabar ahad · Akhbar al-ahad

see also

The Prophet's household, honoured by all Muslims, though the schools draw its boundary differently.

The verse of purification in Surah al-Ahzab sits in a passage addressing his wives, and a hadith records him gathering Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn under a cloak and praying for them. Most Sunni scholars therefore include both the wives and that close family, and many add the wider clan of Banu Hashim who are forbidden to take zakat. Twelver Shia restrict the term to the five of the cloak and the Imams descended from them. Loving them is agreed; the boundary is not.

also written Ahlul Bayt · Ahl ul Bayt · Ahle Bait · Ahlul Bait · Ahl al-Bait · People of the House

see also

People who lived without a prophet's message reaching them, and the question of how they are judged.

The Qur'an says We do not punish until We have sent a messenger (Qur'an 17:15), which every school takes as the starting point. The Ash'ari position is that such a person is not punished, because obligation begins when the message arrives, while Maturidis hold that reason alone still obliges a person to recognise the Creator. A well known group of hadiths describes them being tested on the Day of Judgement itself, and many scholars, including within the Hanbali tradition, hold that view. What all sides agree on is that these are cases for Allah to judge, and not a category for living people to sort each other into.

also written Ahlul Fatrah · Ahl al-Fatra · Ahlulfatra · Fatrah · People of the interval · Those who never heard the message

see also

The main body of Muslims who follow the Prophet's way and the practice of his companions.

The name joins two things: the sunnah, and the jama'ah, the community that held to it. In creed the Sunni world recognises three schools, Ash'ari, Maturidi and Athari; in law it recognises four, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. Difference inside those boundaries is old and normal, and is not the same thing as stepping outside them.

also written Ahlus Sunnah · Ahl as-Sunnah · Ahle Sunnat · Ahlus Sunnah wal Jamaah · Ahl Sunnah wal Jamaah · Sunni

see also

The Prophet's wife, daughter of Abu Bakr, and one of the greatest scholars among the Companions.

She narrated over two thousand hadith, much of it about his life at home, and senior Companions came to her with questions of law and inheritance. When she was accused of adultery by rumour, the community was left in suspense for about a month before verses in Surah an-Nur cleared her and set the rule that such a charge needs four witnesses. She later took a side in the first civil war and afterwards spoke of it with open regret. She died in Madinah and is buried in al-Baqi.

also written Aisha · Ayesha · A'ishah · Ayshah · Aishah bint Abi Bakr · Ayse

see also

The appointed term of a life or a nation, which does not arrive early or run late.

The Qur'an says that when their term comes they cannot delay it by an hour, nor bring it forward (Qur'an 7:34). It is why a believer can take medicine and take cover without any contradiction: means are commanded, outcomes are decreed. The reports that keeping ties of kinship lengthens a life are explained as blessing placed in the time given, or as what stands in the angels' record rather than in Allah's knowledge.

also written Ajel · Ajl · Ajal musamma · Appointed term · Appointed time of death · Lifespan

see also

The hereafter: everything after death, from the grave to the final settling in Paradise or the Fire.

The Qur'an pairs it constantly with the dunya, the near life, and says the hereafter is better and more lasting (Qur'an 87:17). Belief in it is one of the six articles of faith. It is not an escape from this world; the same Qur'an teaches the believer to ask for good in both.

also written Aakhirah · Akhira · Akhirat · Aakhirat · Akheerah · Hereafter

see also

Character: the settled dispositions a person acts from before they have time to think.

The Qur'an describes the Prophet peace be upon him as being upon a great character (Qur'an 68:4), and he said he was sent to complete good character, in a report from Imam Ahmad. He also said the most complete believers in faith are the best of them in character, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Scholars hold that character can be trained, which is the whole reason tazkiyah exists. Nobody is stuck with the temper they were born with.

also written Akhlaaq · Akhlak · Ahlak · Ahlaq · Khuluq · Husn al-khuluq

see also

The seven modes in which the Qur'an was revealed, an ease for the community; what a mode is stays disputed.

The Prophet said the Qur'an was sent down in seven ahruf, and the report appears in the most reliable collections. What an harf actually is has been argued over for centuries, with dozens of explanations offered and none settled. The ahruf are not the same thing as the ten qira'at, though the readings preserve part of what the ahruf allowed.

also written Ahruf · Ahruf as-Sabah · Sab'a ahruf · seven ahruf · seven letters · seven modes

see also

Al-Nawawi's short collection of foundational hadiths, the first hadith text most students memorise.

It is called the Forty and usually contains forty two, since al-Nawawi added a couple beyond his original count. He chose reports that each carry a large share of the religion, opening with the hadith on intention. Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali added eight more and wrote the standard commentary, Jami' al-Ulum wa al-Hikam.

also written Arbaeen Nawawi · Arbain Nawawi · Nawawi's Forty · Forty Hadith · 40 Hadith Nawawi · Al-Arbaun al-Nawawiyyah

see also

The seven verse opening surah, recited in the prayer; most schools require it in every unit.

Its names include the Opening, the Mother of the Book, and the seven oft repeated verses. It is a prayer spoken in the second person: praise first, then a single request, for guidance on the straight path. The schools differ over whether the basmalah counts as its first verse, which is why the seven verses are numbered differently in different mushafs. They differ again over whether someone praying behind an imam recites it: the Hanafis hold that the imam's recitation stands for him.

also written Fatiha · Fateha · Fatihah · Al-Fatiha · Surah Fatiha · Suratul Fatihah

see also

The first civil war among Muslims, from the killing of Uthman to the death of Ali.

Fitnah means a fire that tests metal, and then any trial that separates people. It ran from the thirty fifth to the fortieth year of the Hijrah: the murder of Uthman, the Battle of the Camel, Siffin, the failed arbitration, and the breaking away of the Kharijites who then killed Ali. Sunni scholarship holds that both sides were Companions acting on interpretation, that Ali was closer to the truth, and that the settled adab is to restrain the tongue about what happened.

also written First Fitna · Fitnah · First Civil War · Al-Fitna al-Kubra · Fitna al-Ula · Battle of the Camel

see also

Everything real that lies beyond the reach of the senses, known only because Allah reported it.

The Qur'an opens by describing the God fearing as those who believe in the unseen (Qur'an 2:3). It covers Allah Himself, the angels, the jinn, the grave, the Day of Judgement, Paradise and the Fire. Scholars call these matters sam'iyyat, things received by report, because reason can accept them but could never have discovered them. Claiming private access to the unseen, through stars or cards or spirits, is claiming something the Qur'an reserves to Allah.

also written Ghayb · Ghaib · Gayb · Ghaeb · Gaib · The unseen

see also

The four main hadith collections of Twelver Shia Islam, a separate corpus from the Sunni six books.

They are al-Kafi by al-Kulayni, Man la yahduruhu al-Faqih by Ibn Babawayh, and al-Tahdhib and al-Istibsar by al-Tusi. They record reports from the Prophet and from the Imams, whose sayings carry authority in that tradition. The grading vocabulary overlaps with the Sunni one without matching it: a chain is judged partly by whether its narrators held the Imami creed, and the term muwaththaq marks a reliable narrator who did not.

also written Kutub Arbaa · Kutub al-Arbaah · Kutub e Arba · The Four Books · Four books Shia · Al-Kafi

see also

The Prophet's cousin and son in law, raised by him, and the fourth caliph.

He was the first child to accept Islam and slept in the Prophet's bed on the night of the Hijrah so the assassins would think he was still there. He married Fatimah, carried the banner at Khaybar, and was known for both learning and courage. His caliphate, from the thirty fifth to the fortieth year, was consumed by the first civil war; he moved the capital to Kufa and was killed in its mosque. Sunnis count him the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs; Shia hold him to be the first Imam and the rightful successor from the start.

also written Ali · Ali ibn Abu Talib · Hazrat Ali · Imam Ali · Ali bin Abi Talib · Aliyy

see also

The year an army with an elephant marched on the Ka'bah and was destroyed, around 570.

Abrahah, ruling Yemen, came to pull the Ka'bah down so pilgrims would come to his own church instead. Surah al-Fil describes birds pelting the army with stones of baked clay until they were left like chewed straw. The Prophet was born in that year or close to it, and Arabs dated events from it for a generation afterwards. Abd al-Muttalib's answer to Abrahah is famous: the House has a Lord who will protect it.

also written Aam al-Fil · Year of the Elephant · Am ul Fil · Amul Feel · Aam ul Feel · Abraha

see also

The living practice of Madinah, treated by Malik as evidence that can outweigh a single chain report.

Malik's argument was that an act performed by a whole city in the Prophet's own town, generation after generation, reaches us by mass practice rather than by one man's memory. The Malikis therefore give it weight in law. The other three schools do not accept it as binding and give priority to the authentic report. The disagreement is about how transmission works, not about respect for the Sunnah.

also written Amal ahl al-Madina · Amal ahlul Madinah · Amal e ahl e Madina · Practice of the people of Madinah · Madinan practice · Ijma ahl al-Madinah

see also

A trust: anything placed in your care that you must return, or use exactly as agreed.

The Qur'an commands rendering trusts back to those they belong to. Legally, someone holding an amanah is not liable for loss that occurs without negligence, which is what separates a deposit from a loan or from property seized. The word is also used morally, for the trust of life, of knowledge and of public office, and its opposite is khiyanah, betrayal, which the Prophet named among the signs of hypocrisy.

also written Amana · Amaanah · Amanat · Emanet · Amaanat · Amanaat

see also

The parables of the Qur'an: everyday images used to make an unseen truth visible.

A spider's house for false reliance, a lamp in a niche for light upon light, ash scattered by the wind for deeds without faith. The Qur'an says it sets out such comparisons for people so that they may reflect. Reading them as pictures rather than as puzzles to decode is usually the point.

also written Amthal · Amthaal · Amsal · Mathal · Misal · parables of the Quran

see also

A chain that says only from so and so, without stating that the narrator actually heard the report.

Such a chain is accepted if the narrator is not known for tadlis and could plausibly have met his source. Al-Bukhari held that a proven meeting must be established; Muslim held that living in the same period with the possibility of meeting is enough, and argued the point in the introduction to his Sahih. The disagreement is narrow, but it changes the verdict on a good number of chains.

also written Ananah · An'ana · Anana · Anaana · Muan'an · Muanan

see also

The Muslims of Madinah who took in the emigrants from Makkah and shared everything with them.

The word means the helpers. They were the two tribes of Aws and Khazraj, long at war until Islam reconciled them. The Prophet paired each emigrant with a host in a formal bond of brotherhood, and the Qur'an says they preferred others over themselves even while in need. He told them that love of the Ansar is a mark of faith and dislike of them a mark of hypocrisy, and he died and was buried among them.

also written Ansaar · Ansari · Al-Ansar · Helpers · Ansar of Madinah · Aws

see also

The set of things a Muslim holds to be true, as opposed to the things a Muslim does.

The root means to tie a knot, so aqidah is what the heart is tied to and does not untie. It covers Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree. Fiqh answers what you do; aqidah answers what you hold true.

also written Aqeedah · Aqida · Aqeeda · Aqeedat · Itiqad · I'tiqad

see also

The sacrifice offered for a newborn, customarily on the seventh day, with the naming and the shaving of the head.

The reports name two sheep for a boy and one for a girl, and the majority treat it as a strong sunnah rather than an obligation; the Zahiris held it obligatory. It is done on the seventh day where that is possible, and it is not invalid later. The head is shaved and something is given in charity, and the child is named. Nothing in it requires expense a family does not have, and a family that cannot afford it owes nothing.

also written Aqeeqah · Aqiqa · Akikah · Aqeeqa · Aqiqah sacrifice · Newborn sacrifice

see also

The oaths of the Qur'an, where Allah swears by the dawn, the pen, the fig, the soul.

The oath usually points at what follows it, so the thing sworn by is a clue to the truth being affirmed. The Prophet taught that people may swear only by Allah, and this is no contradiction: the Creator may swear by whatever He has made. Ibn al-Qayyim's at-Tibyan is the classic study of the subject.

also written Aqsam · Aqsaam · Qasam · Qasm · oaths in the Quran · Quran oaths

see also

The open plain east of Makkah where pilgrims gather on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah.

The small hill within it is called Jabal ar-Rahmah, the mount of mercy, and the farewell sermon was delivered nearby. Its day is the climax of the hajj. For Muslims not on hajj, fasting the day of Arafah is a strongly recommended sunnah described as expiating the year before and the year after; pilgrims themselves do not fast it.

also written Arafat · Arafa · Mount Arafat · Jabal ar-Rahmah · day of Arafah · Yawm Arafah

see also

The six articles of faith: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.

They are listed together in the hadith of Jibril, recorded in Sahih Muslim, when the Prophet peace be upon him is asked what faith is. The Qur'an gathers most of them in a single verse about the believers (Qur'an 2:285). These six are the frame, and almost every other question of creed is a detail hanging inside one of them.

also written Arkan ul Iman · Arkanul Iman · Six pillars of faith · Six articles of faith · Pillars of iman · Usul al-Iman

see also

The Throne of Allah, the greatest created thing, above the heavens and carried by angels.

The Qur'an says His Throne was upon the water before the heavens and the earth were made (Qur'an 11:7), and describes angels carrying it and surrounding it with praise (Qur'an 40:7). Sunni scholars affirm it as a real created thing and warn against imagining that Allah needs it or is contained by it. The Prophet peace be upon him said that al-Firdaws, the highest part of Paradise, lies directly beneath it.

also written Al-Arsh · Arash · Ars · Arshullah · Arsh e Ilahi · The Throne

see also

The event or question a particular verse was revealed in answer to.

Knowing the occasion often makes a verse click into place, and it guards against reading a narrow ruling as a sweeping one. These occasions reach us only through narrations, so they are weighed like any report, and a great many verses have no occasion attached at all. The working rule for most scholars is that the lesson lies in the general wording, not in the particular incident.

also written Asbab al-Nuzul · Asbab un Nuzul · Asbabun Nuzul · Sabab an-Nuzul · Shan e Nuzul · Shan-e-Nuzool

see also

A Sunni school of creed founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, defending orthodox belief with reasoned argument.

Al-Ash'ari trained among the Mu'tazila and then left them, turning their own methods toward defending the positions of the people of hadith. The school became associated with Shafi'i and Maliki scholarship, and with figures such as al-Ghazali, al-Razi and al-Nawawi. On the difficult attribute verses it tends toward interpretation or consignment rather than literal wording. It is one of the three creed schools recognised within Ahl al-Sunnah.

also written Ashari · Ashaari · Asharite · Ashariyyah · Asha'ira · Ash'ariyya

see also

Ten Companions named together in one narration as promised Paradise while still alive.

They are Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, Talhah, az-Zubayr, Abd ar-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Sa'id ibn Zayd and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah. The point is not that only ten were promised Paradise; others, including Khadijah, Fatimah, Bilal and the people of Badr, were given similar news in separate reports. These ten are simply the ones listed in a single hadith, which is why they are remembered as a set.

also written Ashara Mubashara · Asharah Mubasharah · Ashra Mubashra · Ten Promised Paradise · Ashara mubashareen · Asharatul Mubashshara

see also

The signs that come before the Day of Judgement, sorted by scholars into minor and major.

The Qur'an says its signs have already come (Qur'an 47:18), which commentators read as the sending of the final Prophet. The minor signs are gradual changes in society described across the hadith literature; the major ones are the ten listed in a report in Sahih Muslim, among them the Dajjal, the descent of Isa, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the beast, the smoke, the sun rising from the west, and a fire that drives people to their final gathering. Reading current events as the fulfilment of signs is an old habit, and every attempt to put a date on it has been wrong so far.

also written Ashrat as-Saah · Alamat al-Qiyamah · Alamat as-Sa'ah · Signs of the Hour · Signs of Qiyamah · End times signs

see also

The tenth of Muharram, a day the Prophet fasted for the deliverance of Musa from Pharaoh.

Arriving in Madinah he found the Jews fasting it and said that he had more right to Musa than they did. Fasting it is recommended and is reported to expiate the previous year; he intended to add the ninth as well, so most fast both. It is also the day Husayn was killed at Karbala in the sixty first year. Sunnis do not treat it as a day of mourning ritual, while Twelver Shia observe it as the central commemoration of that loss.

also written Ashoora · Aashura · Ashurah · Yawm Ashura · Ashura day · Asure

see also

Allah's names and attributes, affirmed as He described them, without denial and without resemblance to creation.

The Qur'an gives Allah names and describes Him with attributes, and it also says there is nothing like Him (Qur'an 42:11). Sunni theology holds both halves at once: affirm what He said about Himself, and do not picture it as a larger version of something created. How far to explain the more difficult descriptions is exactly where the Sunni schools of creed part company.

also written Asma was-Sifat · Asma wal Sifat · Asmaa wa Sifaat · Sifat · Sifaat · Names and Attributes

see also

The eight groups the Qur'an names as the only lawful recipients of zakat.

They are the poor, the needy, those employed to collect it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing those in bondage, the debt burdened, the cause of Allah, and the stranded traveller. The list is fixed by a single verse, which is why most scholars hold that zakat cannot be spent on a mosque building or a general good cause the way sadaqah can. Scholars differ over how widely the seventh category may be read.

also written Asnaf al-zakat · eight categories · eight recipients · Masarif al-zakat · who can receive zakat · Mustahiq

see also

A report from a Companion or a follower rather than from the Prophet himself.

The word means a trace or a footprint, what is left behind after someone passes. Most scholars use athar for what stops at a Companion or a Tabi'i, and hadith for what reaches the Prophet, though some early scholars used athar for any report at all. Athar matters because Companion practice often shows what a hadith meant in the room where it was said.

also written Athaar · Aathar · Asar · Asaar · Aasar · Aathaar

see also

The Sunni creed school that keeps to the wording of the texts and avoids theological speculation.

Athar means a narration, and the approach is to affirm what the Qur'an and Sunnah say about Allah in their own words, without figurative interpretation and without asking how. It is associated with Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and later with Ibn Taymiyyah and with much modern Salafi thought. Along with the Ash'aris and Maturidis it is one of the three recognised Sunni creed schools, and the argument between the three is old, sharp, and internal.

also written Atharis · Athariyyah · Atheri · Ahl al-Hadith · Ahlul Hadith · Traditionalist creed

see also

A verse of the Qur'an, and in ordinary Arabic a sign.

The same word is used for the signs of Allah in creation, which is why a verse is called a sign rather than a line. Most scholars hold that verse endings were fixed by the Prophet's own recitation; the numbers printed in the margins were added later as an aid. The Hafs printing counts 6,236 verses, and other counting traditions divide a few verses differently and reach slightly different totals.

also written Aya · Ayat · Aayah · Aayat · Ayaat · Ayahs

see also

A hadith which at no stage of its chain has fewer than two narrators.

The word here means scarce, hard to come by. Aziz sits between gharib, which has a single narrator somewhere in the chain, and mashhur, which has three or more. The category counts how many routes exist; it does not by itself say whether the hadith is sound.

also written Azeez · Aziiz · Aziz hadith · Azeez hadeeth · Two narrators · Aaziz

see also

B

The resurrection: bodies raised and souls returned, so that everyone stands for judgement.

The Qur'an answers the objection directly, asking who will give life to bones after they have crumbled, and replying that He who produced them the first time will (Qur'an 36:78-79). The gathering that follows is called the hashr, on an open plain where nobody is missed or overlooked. Sunni belief is that the raising is bodily and not only spiritual.

also written Bath · Baath · Ba'ath · Yawm al-Bath · Resurrection · Raising of the dead

see also

The first major battle, in year two, where about three hundred Muslims defeated a much larger force.

It began as an attempt to intercept a caravan and became a pitched fight against roughly a thousand Quraysh. The Qur'an calls the day the Furqan, the day of separation, and describes angels sent to support the believers. Fathers faced sons and brothers faced brothers in it. Those who fought at Badr, the Badriyyun, hold a rank of their own; the Prophet indicated that Allah had looked upon them and forgiven them.

also written Battle of Badr · Ghazwat Badr · Jang e Badr · Badar · Bedir · Badr al-Kubra

see also

The first dynasty of caliphs, ruling from Damascus for about ninety years after the Rashidun.

It began with Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan, a Companion and scribe of revelation, and turned the caliphate into an inherited office. Under them the state reached Spain in the west and the Indus in the east, Arabic became the language of administration, coinage was reformed, and the Dome of the Rock was built. Muslim assessment of them is mixed and always has been. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, the exception nearly everyone praises, came from this family.

also written Umayyads · Umayyad · Umayyad Caliphate · Bani Umayyah · Banu Umayya · Emeviler

see also

Blessing: a quality Allah puts in a thing so that a small amount goes further than it should.

The Qur'an speaks of blessings opened from the sky and the earth for a town that believes (Qur'an 7:96), and quotes Isa saying he was made blessed wherever he is (Qur'an 19:31). Barakah attaches to time, food, wealth, knowledge and people, and it is not measured in quantity: an hour with barakah does the work of three. The Sunnah connects it with naming Allah before eating, honesty in trade, early mornings, and gratitude.

also written Baraka · Barakat · Barkat · Barakaat · Mubarak · Tabarak

see also

The state between death and the resurrection, where the soul waits after the body is buried.

The word means a barrier or partition. The Qur'an uses it of the one who begs to be returned to life and is refused: behind them is a barrier until the Day they are raised (Qur'an 23:100). It is a real condition, with ease or with distress, and its details are not measurable by anything we can observe from this side.

also written Barzak · Barzah · Barzagh · Alam al-Barzakh · Life in the grave · Between death and resurrection

see also

The opening line In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, found before nearly every surah.

It stands at the head of 113 surahs; at-Tawbah alone has none. It also appears inside the Qur'an as the opening of Sulayman's letter in Surah an-Naml. The schools differ over whether it is a verse of al-Fatihah and whether it is said aloud in prayer, which is why practice varies from one mosque to the next.

also written Bismillah · Basmala · Bismilah · Bismillahir Rahmanir Raheem · Bismillah ir-Rahman ir-Rahim · Basmalla

see also

The first clash with Byzantine forces, in year eight, where three appointed commanders fell in turn.

The Prophet named Zayd ibn Harithah to lead, then Ja'far ibn Abi Talib if Zayd fell, then Abdullah ibn Rawahah if Ja'far fell. All three were killed. Khalid ibn al-Walid, newly Muslim, took up the banner and extracted the army intact, and the Prophet called him a sword among the swords of Allah. He is reported to have described the deaths to the Companions in Madinah while the battle was still being fought far away. He did not go himself, so by the strict usage it is a sariyyah rather than a ghazwah.

also written Mutah · Mootah · Muta · Ghazwat Mutah · Battle of Muta · Jang e Mutah

see also

Sale: the exchange of property for property by mutual consent.

The Qur'an states that God has permitted trade and forbidden riba, and the Prophet himself worked as a merchant before prophethood. A valid sale needs a known price, a known item the seller can actually deliver, ownership or authority to sell it, and consent untouched by deception. Fiqh names many specific forms, among them salam, paid now and delivered later, and murabahah, sold at a disclosed markup.

also written Bay · Bai · Baye · Bai' · Buyu · Buyoo

see also

A pledge of allegiance, given to a ruler, or in Sufi orders to a spiritual guide.

The word comes from bay', a sale, since the one who pledges gives loyalty and receives protection in return. The Qur'an records the pledge under the tree and the pledge of the believing women, and the Prophet took bay'ah on obedience in what is good, a condition scholars stress: there is no obedience to a creature in disobedience to the Creator. In Sufi orders bay'ah to a shaykh is a commitment to a path of training, which is a different use of the same word.

also written Bayah · Baya · Bayat · Baiah · Bai'ah · Biat

see also

Two secret pledges by men of Madinah that opened the way for the Hijrah.

They were made at a mountain pass near Mina during the pilgrimage season. In the first, twelve men promised to worship none but Allah and to keep away from theft, adultery, infanticide and slander, and Mus'ab ibn Umayr was sent back with them as teacher. A year later roughly seventy men and two women pledged to protect him as they would protect their own families, knowing exactly what it would cost. Within months the Muslims of Makkah began slipping away to Madinah.

also written Bayat al Aqabah · Baiat ul Aqabah · Pledge of Aqabah · Pledges of al-Aqaba · Bayah Aqabah · Second Pledge of Aqaba

see also

Innovation in religion: introducing an act of worship that has no basis in what was revealed.

The Prophet peace be upon him said that whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that is not from it will have it rejected, in Bukhari and Muslim. Everyone agrees that new things in worldly life are not the subject; nobody calls a printing press or a microphone bid'ah. Scholars differ on the categories: many, following al-Shafi'i and al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam, sort innovations into praiseworthy and blameworthy, while others hold that whatever is correctly called bid'ah in religion is blameworthy, and the good cases were never bid'ah to begin with.

also written Bidah · Bidat · Bid'at · Bidaa · Biddah · Bida

see also

An enslaved Abyssinian tortured for his faith, freed by Abu Bakr, and the first to call the adhan.

His owner pinned him under a rock in the midday heat of Makkah and he answered only with one word, ahad, one. Abu Bakr bought him and set him free. When the Muslims settled in Madinah and needed a way to gather people, he was given the call to prayer, and on the day Makkah was taken he climbed onto the Ka'bah to make it. The Prophet told him he had heard his footsteps ahead of him in Paradise, and Bilal explained he prayed after every wudu.

also written Bilal · Bilal ibn Rabah · Bilal bin Rabah · Bilal al-Habashi · Bilal Habashi · Belal

see also

D

A hadith that fails one of the conditions of soundness, through a broken chain or a faulty narrator.

Weak does not mean false. It means the report did not arrive with enough support to be relied upon. Weakness has degrees, from a slight gap that other chains can repair, up to a narrator accused of lying, which nothing can repair. Whether a weak hadith may be used to encourage good deeds is an old disagreement among scholars rather than a settled rule.

also written Daif · Da'eef · Daeef · Dhaif · Dhaeef · Dha'eef

see also

The accuracy of a narrator: how well he held the report, in memory or in a guarded book.

Two kinds are recognised: precision of the chest, meaning memory, and precision of the book, meaning a written copy kept safely and not lent out carelessly. Light weakness here drops a hadith from sahih to hasan. Heavy weakness, where a man's errors outnumber his sound reports, drops it further.

also written Dhabt · Zabt · Dabit · Daabit · Dhabit · Dabt al-sadr

see also

The false messiah who appears near the end of time, claiming godhood and testing people with power.

He is not named in the Qur'an, but the reports about him are so numerous that Sunni scholars treat them as certain. He is described as one eyed, with disbelief written between his eyes, given power to show wonders and to control provision, and finally killed by Isa. The Prophet peace be upon him said that every prophet warned his people about him, and taught the opening verses of Surah al-Kahf as protection.

also written Dajaal · Dajal · Dajjaal · Dajall · Al-Masih ad-Dajjal · Masih Dajjal

see also

A compensating sacrifice owed for omitting a required rite of hajj or breaking a rule of ihram.

The word means blood. It is usually a sheep or goat, slaughtered in the sanctuary and given to the poor there, and for some breaches a person may instead fast or feed the needy. The schools differ over which acts are required rather than recommended, so an omission that costs a dam in one school may cost nothing in another. A dam repairs a shortfall; a hady is part of the pilgrimage itself.

also written Damm · Dum · penalty sacrifice · compensation sacrifice · hajj penalty · Dam for missing wajib

see also

Necessity: the state in which something forbidden becomes permitted in order to preserve life.

The Qur'an allows a starving person to eat forbidden meat without sin, provided he is not seeking to transgress. Jurists built a maxim on it, that necessity makes the forbidden permitted, and bounded it with a second, that necessity is measured strictly by its extent. Hardship and inconvenience are not darurah; the classical threshold is real danger to life, limb, mind, lineage or property.

also written Darura · Dharurah · Zarurah · Darurat · Dharura · Zarurat

see also

Meat from an animal slaughtered in the Islamic way, with the name of God pronounced over it.

The throat is cut swiftly with a sharp blade, severing the windpipe and the blood vessels, and the animal must be alive and treated gently beforehand; the Prophet ordered the blade to be sharpened, the animal spared distress, and the knife kept out of its sight. The Qur'an also permits the food of the People of the Book, and scholars differ over whether ordinary commercial meat in Jewish and Christian countries falls under that permission. Pork, blood, carrion and anything dedicated to other than God remain forbidden either way.

also written Zabiha · Zabihah · Dhabiha · Zabeeha · Dhabh · Zabh

see also

Remembrance of Allah, in set phrases and in the wider habit of not forgetting Him.

The Qur'an says hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah (Qur'an 13:28) and tells believers to remember Him and He will remember them (Qur'an 2:152). In practice dhikr covers the short phrases such as subhan Allah and la ilaha illa Allah, the morning and evening adhkar, reciting the Qur'an, and the wider state of living aware of Him. Sufi orders add group and audible forms, and that is where scholars disagree about method, not about dhikr itself.

also written Zikr · Zikir · Zikar · Thikr · Dhkr · Zekr

see also

The historic covenant under which non Muslims in a Muslim state kept their religion and protection.

The word means liability or covenant, and ahl al-dhimmah are the people it covered. In exchange for jizyah they were exempt from military service and from zakat, kept their own courts in matters of personal law, and had their lives, property and places of worship protected; the Prophet warned that whoever wrongs a covenanted person will find the Prophet himself his opponent on the Day of Judgement. It was a premodern arrangement of defined but unequal status, and most contemporary scholars treat it as superseded by common citizenship.

also written Dhimma · Zimmah · Zimmi · Dhimmi · Ahl al-dhimma · Ahl adh-dhimmah

see also

Blood money: compensation paid to a victim's family for a killing or an injury.

The Qur'an prescribes it for accidental killing, alongside the freeing of a slave, and it is also what a family receives when they waive qisas for a deliberate one. The classical measure is one hundred camels, which jurists converted into gold, silver or currency, with fixed fractions for the loss of an eye, a hand or a tooth. In the classical rules the payment falls on the killer's kin group, the 'aqilah, an early form of shared insurance.

also written Diya · Diyat · Khoon baha · Diyya · Diyet · Blood money

see also

Asking Allah directly, in any language, at any time, for anything permitted.

The Qur'an says call on Me and I will answer you (Qur'an 40:60), and the Prophet peace be upon him said du'a is worship itself, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Scholars describe three possible answers: the thing asked for, something equal or better kept back for later, or a harm turned away. He also warned against impatience, saying a servant is answered as long as he does not say I asked and was not answered, in Bukhari and Muslim.

also written Dua · Duaa · Du'aa · Dooa · Doa · Supplication

see also

A voluntary prayer of two to eight rak'ahs in the mid-morning, after sunrise and before noon.

Its time opens once the sun has risen clearly above the horizon and closes shortly before midday. The Prophet described a charity due from every joint in the body each morning, and said two rak'ahs of duha are enough for all of it. Some call the earliest part of that window ishraq, and in the subcontinent it is often called chasht.

also written Doha · Dhuha · Salat ad-duha · Chasht · Chaasht · Ishraq

see also

The nearer life: this world, which is not condemned in itself, only when it becomes the whole aim.

The word means the nearer or the lower, and names this life set against the one that comes after. The Qur'an describes it as play, amusement and mutual boasting (Qur'an 57:20), and elsewhere tells a man not to forget his share of it. What is criticised is preferring it (Qur'an 87:16-17), not eating well, working, or loving your family. A useful reading: dunya is not the place, it is the place taken as final.

also written Duniya · Dunia · Donya · Dunyaa · Hubb al-dunya · Love of dunya

see also

F

The old question of whether a weak hadith may be used to encourage deeds already known to be good.

Three positions exist. Some scholars refuse it outright, holding that nothing should be attributed to the Prophet unless it is established. The majority allow it under conditions: the weakness must be light, the deed must already rest on something authentic, and nobody should believe the Prophet actually said the words. All three agree that a weak hadith does not establish a point of belief or a ruling, though some early jurists preferred a weak report to their own reasoning when a chapter held nothing else.

also written Fadail al-Amal · Fadhail e Amal · Fazail e Amal · Fada'il al-a'mal · Fadail amal · Virtues of deeds

see also

The five obligatory prayers: dawn, past midday, afternoon, just after sunset, and night.

Fajr runs from true dawn until sunrise. Dhuhr begins once the sun has passed its highest point. Asr fills the later afternoon, Maghrib begins at sunset, and Isha begins once the twilight has gone and lasts until dawn. The schools differ over exactly when Asr begins, and over which twilight closes the time of Maghrib, which is why mosques in the same city sometimes call these times an hour apart.

also written Fajar · Subh · Subuh · Zuhr · Zohr · Duhr

see also

Obligatory: required by decisive evidence, and sinful to abandon without an excuse.

The five daily prayers, the fast of Ramadan and zakat are fard. Hanafis reserve the word for what is proved beyond doubt and use wajib for what rests on a single strong report, so for them denying a fard is disbelief while denying a wajib is not. The other three schools treat fard and wajib as two names for one thing, which explains a good deal of apparent disagreement in books.

also written Fardh · Farz · Fardhu · Fardu · Faridah · Faraid

see also

An individual obligation: every responsible Muslim must perform it personally.

Prayer, fasting Ramadan, zakat when you own the nisab, and hajj once if you are able. Nobody can discharge these on your behalf, and another person doing them does not lift them from you. Learning enough to practise your own religion is also fard 'ayn, which is why the basics of purification, prayer and honest earning are everybody's business and not only the scholars'.

also written Fard ayn · Fardh ain · Farz-i ayn · Fardu ain · Fard al-ayn · Fardain

see also

A communal obligation: if enough people carry it out, it is lifted from everyone else.

The funeral prayer, memorising the Qur'an, medicine, and returning a greeting given to a group all fall here. If nobody does it, everyone capable shares the blame; once it is covered, it becomes merely recommended for the rest. Much of what a community actually needs, from judges and doctors to those who wash the dead, is organised under this single heading.

also written Fard kifaya · Fardh kifayah · Farz-i kifaye · Fardu kifayah · Fard al-kifayah · Kifayah

see also

Annulment: a judge dissolving a marriage for a defect or a failure of duty.

Grounds recognised across the schools include serious undisclosed illness, impotence, insanity, desertion, imprisonment, failure to maintain, and harm. Malikis are the broadest here, allowing dissolution for harm in general, which is why courts in many countries follow them on this point even where another school prevails. Faskh differs from talaq because it uses up none of the husband's pronouncements, and from khul' because it requires no payment from the wife.

also written Fask · Faskh nikah · Fasakh · Fesih · Tafriq · Tatliq

see also

The Prophet's return to Makkah in year eight, taken almost without a fight.

Quraysh had broken the Hudaybiyah truce, and he came with an army large enough to make resistance pointless. He entered with his head bowed low over his mount, cleared the idols from around the Ka'bah, and told the people who had driven him out and killed his family that they could go, there was no blame on them today. Surah an-Nasr, about people entering the religion in crowds, belongs to this moment. He also declared that there is no hijrah after the conquest.

also written Conquest of Mecca · Fath Makka · Fatah Makkah · Fath e Makkah · Opening of Mecca · Fatih Mekke

see also

The Prophet's youngest daughter, wife of Ali and mother of Hasan and Husayn.

She lived plainly; the famous exchange in which she asked her father for a servant and was taught words of remembrance instead is well known. He said she was a part of him, and that whoever angers her angers him. In his final illness he whispered something that made her weep and then something that made her smile: that he was dying, and that she would be the first of his household to follow him. She died about six months later, in her twenties.

also written Fatima · Fatimah az-Zahra · Fatima Zahra · Fatimah bint Muhammad · Fatma · Fatema

see also

A scholar's answer to a specific question: advice, not a court judgement.

The one who gives it is a mufti and the one who asks is a mustafti. A fatwa compels nobody, it can differ from another qualified scholar's fatwa without either being wrong, and a good one depends closely on the asker's circumstances, which is why lifting someone else's fatwa off the internet can mislead you badly. A judge's ruling is the opposite: binding, and it settles the case for everyone in it.

also written Fatwah · Fetva · Fatawa · Fataawa · Fatwas · Mufti

see also

Feeding a poor person for each fast that a person is permanently unable to keep or make up.

The Qur'an mentions it for those who can only fast with great hardship, which scholars apply to the very old and the chronically ill with no prospect of recovery. It is one meal or its value for each missed day, given to someone in need. Anyone who expects to recover owes qada instead, and should not pay fidyah to avoid fasting.

also written Fidya · Fidiyah · Fitya · Fidyah for fasting · ransom · feeding for missed fasts

see also

The human effort to work out Islamic law from its sources, and the rulings that result.

The word means understanding. Fiqh is not the same as shari'ah: shari'ah is the guidance God revealed, fiqh is what scholars understood of it, which is why qualified people reach different answers. Books of fiqh nearly all run in the same order: purification and prayer first, then fasting, zakat and hajj, then marriage, trade, inheritance and the courts.

also written Fikh · Feqh · Fiqah · Fikih · Fiqih · Fiqhi

see also

The natural disposition every person is born with, leaning toward recognising one Creator.

The Qur'an speaks of the fitrah of Allah upon which He made people (Qur'an 30:30), and the Prophet peace be upon him said that every child is born upon the fitrah, in Bukhari and Muslim. It is not a memory of doctrine but a leaning, and it is easily covered over by habit and upbringing. In fiqh the same word names the acts of natural cleanliness, which is a separate meaning of one root.

also written Fitra · Fithrah · Fitrat · Fetra · Human nature · Natural disposition

see also

G

Anger, which is not a sin in itself, and is judged by what a person does while holding it.

A man asked the Prophet peace be upon him for advice and was told, do not become angry, and the man kept asking and got the same answer, in Bukhari. He also said the strong man is not the wrestler, but the one who controls himself when angry, in Bukhari and Muslim. The practical instructions include seeking refuge from Shaytan and sitting down if you are standing, in a report collected by Abu Dawud. The Qur'an praises those who restrain anger and pardon people (Qur'an 3:134), which is restraint, not absence.

also written Ghazab · Gadab · Gazab · Ghadhab · Ghussa · Anger

see also

Lowering the gaze: turning your eyes away from what you are not permitted to look at.

The Qur'an instructs believing men, and then believing women, to lower their gaze and guard their chastity (Qur'an 24:30-31). The Prophet peace be upon him told Ali that the first look is his and the second is not, in a report collected by Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Classical scholars treat it as the practical gate of the heart, on the principle that whatever the eye brings in, the heart has to carry. It is a discipline of the second look, not an order to walk with your head down.

also written Ghadd al basar · Ghad al-basar · Ghadhul basar · Gad al basar · Lowering the gaze · Lower your gaze

see also

Heedlessness: not the denial of the truth, but the habit of never getting round to it.

The Qur'an says people's reckoning has drawn near while they turn away heedless (Qur'an 21:1), and describes the heedless as further astray than cattle (Qur'an 7:179). It is the ordinary condition that dhikr exists to interrupt, which is one reason the adhkar are attached to times of day rather than to moods. Ghaflah is rarely a decision. It is what happens by default.

also written Ghafla · Gaflah · Ghafil · Ghaafil · Gafil · Heedlessness

see also

The small cave above Makkah where the Prophet was praying when revelation first came.

It sits near the top of Jabal an-Nur, the mountain of light, a hard climb even now. He used to withdraw there for nights at a time before prophethood, and it was there that Jibril pressed him and said Read. He came home shaking and asked to be covered, and Khadijah wrapped him and told him Allah would never disgrace him. He is not reported to have returned to the cave afterwards, so climbing it is a matter of history, not a rite.

also written Cave of Hira · Hira · Hera · Ghar e Hira · Jabal an-Nur · Jabal al-Nour

see also

The cave south of Makkah where the Prophet and Abu Bakr hid three nights during the Hijrah.

Quraysh had put a price on his head and search parties came close enough for Abu Bakr to see their feet. The Qur'an records the moment in Surah at-Tawbah, calling him the second of two when they were in the cave, and quoting his words to his companion: do not grieve, Allah is with us. The verse is the strongest single proof Sunnis cite for Abu Bakr's rank. Abu Bakr was in his fifties and climbed the mountain in the dark.

also written Cave of Thawr · Ghar e Thawr · Ghar Sur · Jabal Thawr · Thawr · Cave of Thaur

see also

Excessive uncertainty in a contract, which makes the deal invalid.

The Prophet forbade the gharar sale, and the stock examples jurists give are the young of an animal not yet born, and the fish still in the water. The problem is not risk, which every honest trade carries, but not knowing what you are buying, at what price, or whether it exists at all. Minor uncertainty is tolerated, since no contract is perfectly precise. Scholars invoke gharar when questioning conventional insurance and some derivative contracts, and takaful was designed as an answer to it.

also written Gharrar · Garar · Ghara · Gharar fahish · bay al-gharar · uncertainty

see also

A hadith narrated by only one person at some point in its chain.

Gharib means strange, or lone. It is not a criticism in itself: the famous hadith that deeds are judged by intentions is gharib at its start and sits in both Sahihs. The same word has a second and unrelated use, gharib al-hadith, meaning the study of rare and difficult words inside hadith texts.

also written Ghareeb · Garib · Ghareib · Gharib hadith · Ghareeb hadeeth · Fard

see also

The study of the Qur'an's rare or difficult words, and what they meant to their first hearers.

Arabic shifts over time, and words that were everyday in the seventh century can be obscure now. Ibn Abbas is known for explaining such words by citing lines of pre Islamic poetry. Al-Raghib al-Isfahani's Mufradat is the standard reference and is still the first book a student opens on a hard word.

also written Gharib al-Quran · Ghareeb ul Quran · Gharib · Ghareeb · Mufradat · rare words in the Quran

see also

A military expedition the Prophet led in person, as opposed to one he sent out under another.

An expedition he dispatched without going himself is a sariyyah. Historians count the ghazawat in the twenties and the sariyyah in the dozens, though the lists differ, and in most of them no fighting actually occurred. The genre of books recording them is called maghazi, and it is the oldest layer of sirah writing. The word by itself means a raid; it carries no ruling, and it is not a synonym for jihad.

also written Ghazwa · Ghazawat · Ghazwat · Gazwah · Ghazve · Maghazi

see also

Mentioning something about a person, behind their back, that they would dislike hearing.

The Qur'an compares it to eating the flesh of your dead brother (Qur'an 49:12). When the Prophet peace be upon him was asked what if it is true, he answered that if it is true you have backbitten him, and if it is not you have slandered him, in Muslim. Scholars list narrow exceptions, such as warning someone about a business partner or a marriage proposal, or reporting a wrong to a person able to stop it. These exist for need, not for cover.

also written Gheebah · Gheeba · Ghiba · Ghibat · Gheebat · Gibah

see also

The nasal hum carried by nun and meem, held about two counts wherever the rules require it.

It comes out through the nose, not the mouth: pinch your nose and the sound is cut off. It is fullest on a nun or meem carrying a shaddah, which is why those two are called the letters of ghunnah. It also appears inside idgham, ikhfa and iqlab.

also written Ghunna · Gunnah · Ghunnah rules · Ghunna tajweed · nasal sound · nasalisation

see also

The full washing of the whole body that lifts the major state of ritual impurity.

It is required after intercourse or sexual discharge, and at the end of menstruation and postnatal bleeding. It is recommended before Jumu'ah, the two Eids, and entering ihram. At minimum it is an intention and water reaching every part of the skin and hair; the schools differ over whether rinsing the mouth and nose, and rubbing the skin, are obligatory or recommended. A ghusl done properly also counts for wudu.

also written Gusl · Ghusal · Ghusul · Ghust · Gusul · Boy abdesti

see also

H

The ritual state that blocks prayer until it is lifted by wudu or by ghusl.

Minor hadath comes from things like using the toilet or sleeping deeply, and is lifted by wudu. Major hadath comes from sexual discharge, menstruation and postnatal bleeding, and is lifted by ghusl. It is a legal state, not dirt: a person in hadath may be perfectly clean, and a person covered in mud may have valid wudu.

also written Hadas · Hadeth · Hadath asghar · Hadath akbar · minor impurity · major impurity

see also

A report of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did, or quietly approved, passed down through named narrators.

The word means speech, or something newly told. A hadith has two parts: the chain of people who carried it, and the text they carried. A hadith is a report about the Sunnah, so a weak hadith does not become Sunnah by being printed in a book.

also written Hadeeth · Hadis · Hadits · Ahadith · Ahadeeth · Hadees

see also

A hadith in which the Prophet reports words from Allah that are not part of the Qur'an.

The usual account is that the meaning is from Allah and the wording from the Prophet, while the Qur'an is both meaning and wording from Allah. A hadith qudsi is not recited in prayer and carries no claim of inimitability. It is also not automatically authentic; like any hadith it can be sahih, hasan or weak.

also written Hadis Qudsi · Qudsi hadith · Hadeeth Qudsi · Sacred hadith · Divine hadith · Hadith al-Qudsi

see also

Fast recitation that still keeps every rule intact, used mainly when revising memorisation.

Speed itself is allowed; dropping letters, cutting a madd short or blurring word endings is not. A hafiz revising several juz in a day will usually recite in hadr. If the words begin running into each other, the answer is to slow down rather than push on.

also written Hader · Hadar · Hadr recitation · fast recitation · quick recitation · Hadr Quran

see also

The animal offered in Makkah by pilgrims performing tamattu' or qiran, and its meat given away.

The word means a gift brought forward. It is a sheep or goat per pilgrim, or a seventh share of a camel or cow, slaughtered after the stoning on the tenth. The Qur'an says neither the meat nor the blood reaches Allah, only the God consciousness of the giver. It is different from the qurbani offered by Muslims everywhere at Eid, and different again from a dam owed as compensation.

also written Hadi · Hadhy · Hadyi · Hedy · sacrificial animal · hajj sacrifice

see also

In hadith, a master who has memorised a very large number of reports together with their chains.

In everyday speech today hafiz means someone who has memorised the Qur'an, and that use is fine. In hadith books it is a technical rank above muhaddith, given to men like Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, who is often called simply al-Hafiz. The word means one who guards something.

also written Haafiz · Hafidh · Hafidz · Huffaz · Huffadh · Hafez

see also

Someone who has memorised the whole Qur'an and can recite it from memory.

The plural is huffaz and the feminine is hafizah. In the hadith sciences the same title means a scholar who has memorised a vast number of narrations, so it is not always about the Qur'an. It is not a permanent state either: without revision it slips away, which is why huffaz keep reciting for life.

also written Hafiz · Hafidh · Hafez · Haafiz · Hafiza · Hafidha

see also

The reading found in most printed mushafs today, transmitted by Hafs from his teacher Asim of Kufa.

Hafs ibn Sulayman learned it from Asim ibn Abi an-Najud, whose chain runs back through the Companions to the Prophet. It spread with mass printing and is now the default across most of the Muslim world, which is why many readers assume it is the only way the Qur'an is read. Asim's other transmitter, Shu'bah, differs from Hafs in a modest number of places.

also written Hafs · Hafz · Hafs from Asim · Hafs an Aasim · Hafs 'an 'Asim · Asim

see also

The pilgrimage to Makkah in Dhul Hijjah, obligatory once in a lifetime on those who are able.

It is the fifth pillar. The condition of ability, called istita'ah, covers health, safe passage and the money to travel and to leave dependants provided for; someone who lacks these owes nothing. The rites run over several days across Makkah, Mina, Arafah and Muzdalifah, retracing the acts of Ibrahim, Hajar and Isma'il. Umrah can be done at any time of year, but hajj cannot.

also written Haj · Hadj · Hac · Hajj pilgrimage · Haji · Hajji

see also

The only hajj the Prophet performed after it was made obligatory, in year ten.

More than a hundred thousand people came, and he told them to take their rites from him, which is why almost every detail of the hajj is traced to those days. He stood at Arafah and delivered the farewell sermon there. The verse saying the religion has been completed was revealed on that afternoon; when a Jewish man later remarked that such a verse would have been a festival for his people, Umar replied that it came on a day that was already two festivals.

also written Farewell Pilgrimage · Hajjatul Wida · Hijjat al-Wada · Hajj al-Wada · Hajjat ul Wada · Farewell Hajj

see also

Permitted. Anything revelation has not forbidden, which is the great majority of things.

The word means loosed or untied. In ordinary worldly matters the default is permission, so the burden of proof lies on whoever claims a thing is forbidden, not on the person doing it. In food it usually means meat slaughtered properly and free of pork, blood and intoxicants. But halal covers earnings, speech and work at least as much as it covers dinner.

also written Halaal · Hallal · Helal · Halall · Halel · Halial

see also

Shaving the head after the rites, which releases the pilgrim from the state of ihram.

The Prophet asked mercy for those who shave three times and for those who trim once, so shaving is the better of the two for men. Women never shave; they gather their hair and cut about a fingertip's length from the end. It is done after the stoning on the tenth for hajj, and after the sa'i for umrah.

also written Halk · Halaq · Halq or taqsir · shaving the head · shaving after hajj · Hilaq

see also

The Prophet's uncle, called the Lion of Allah, killed at Uhud.

He accepted Islam in anger, hearing that Abu Jahl had abused his nephew, and his conversion changed the balance of pressure on the Muslims in Makkah. He fought at Badr and was killed at Uhud by Wahshi, a man promised his freedom for the deed, and the Prophet was profoundly grieved by the state of his body. Years later Wahshi accepted Islam and was forgiven, though the Prophet asked him to keep his face out of sight. Hamzah is remembered as the chief of the martyrs.

also written Hamza · Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib · Hamza bin Abdul Muttalib · Amir Hamza · Hamzah al-Asad · Lion of Allah

see also

The school of Abu Hanifah, the most widely followed, known for careful reasoning and analogy.

Named for Abu Hanifah al-Nu'man ibn Thabit of Kufa, who died in 150 AH, and set down by his students Abu Yusuf and al-Shaybani. It is the school of most Muslims in Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia, South Asia and much of the Levant and Egypt. Its distinctive features include a strong use of istihsan and of local custom, and a separate ruling category of wajib standing just below fard.

also written Hanafee · Hanefi · Hanfi · Hanafiyyah · Abu Hanifah · Abu Hanifa

see also

The school of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the most text bound of the four, strongest in Arabia.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal died in 241 AH and is remembered as much for his endurance under persecution as for his law. In worship the school stays close to the reports and is cautious about opinion. In transactions it is unusually permissive, holding that any contract is valid unless something forbids it. Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn al-Qayyim wrote from within this school.

also written Hanbalee · Hambali · Hanabila · Hanbaliyyah · Ahmad ibn Hanbal · Imam Ahmad

see also

Forbidden. Leaving it is rewarded, and doing it deliberately is a sin.

The list is far shorter than people assume: shirk, killing, theft, interest, intoxicants, pork, gambling, zina, and injustice to others. Something is haram only on clear evidence, and calling a disputed matter haram is itself a serious step, since the Qur'an warns against declaring things lawful and unlawful without knowledge. The same root also means sacred and inviolable, which is why the mosque in Makkah is al-Masjid al-Haram.

also written Haraam · Harram · Haramm · Harem · Haraam food · forbidden

see also

Envy: wishing a blessing would leave someone, rather than wishing you had one too.

The Qur'an teaches seeking refuge from the evil of an envier when he envies (Qur'an 113:5). Scholars separate blameworthy hasad, which wants the gift removed, from ghibtah, which wants the same gift without wanting anyone stripped of theirs; the second is permitted and even praised. Envy arrives without permission. What is judged is whether a person acts on it or feeds it.

also written Hased · Hasd · Hasid · Haasid · Hasada · Ghibtah

see also

A hadith meeting every condition of sahih except that one narrator's accuracy falls slightly short.

Hasan means good. It is a working grade: acceptable as evidence in law, one step below sahih. Al-Tirmidhi made the term widely used, and later scholars spent great effort defining it, since the line between light weakness and real weakness is a matter of trained judgement.

also written Hassan · Hasen · Hasan hadith · Hasan hadeeth · Hasan li-dhatihi · Hasan lidhatihi

see also

The Prophet's elder grandson, who gave up the caliphate to stop a war between Muslims.

After Ali was killed the people of Iraq pledged to him, and Mu'awiyah held Syria. Rather than fight, he negotiated terms and stepped aside in the forty first year, and that year is called the Year of Unity. The Prophet had said of him, while he was a child on the pulpit, that this son of his is a master and that Allah would reconcile two great parties of Muslims through him. Twelver Shia count him the second Imam, and he is buried in al-Baqi.

also written Hasan · Imam Hasan · Hassan ibn Ali · Al-Hasan · Hasan bin Ali · Hasan al-Mujtaba

see also

A weak hadith raised to the level of hasan because other chains carry the same meaning.

This only works when the weakness is mild, such as a narrator with a poor memory, and never when a narrator is accused of lying. Two or three light chains leaning on one another can hold a report up. Scholars differ over how much support is enough, which is why the same hadith is sometimes graded hasan by one and weak by another.

also written Hasan li ghayrihi · Hasan li ghairih · Hasan lighairihi · Hasan bi ghayrihi · Hasan due to others · Hasan li ghayrih

see also

Al-Tirmidhi's double grading, which later scholars have explained in several different ways.

Read literally it sounds like calling one thing good and excellent at once. The best known explanation, from Ibn Hajar, is that where the hadith has a single chain the phrase means some scholars judged it hasan and others sahih, and where it has several chains one is hasan and another sahih. Other scholars read it differently. It is safest to treat the phrase as meaning acceptable rather than as a precise grade.

also written Hasan saheeh · Hasanun sahih · Hasan sahih gharib · Tirmidhi hasan sahih · Hasan-sahih · Hasan saheeh gharib

see also

Whim: personal desire raised high enough that a person follows it instead of the evidence.

The Qur'an asks whether you have seen the one who has taken his desire as his god (Qur'an 45:23), and promises the Garden to whoever feared standing before his Lord and restrained the self from its whim (Qur'an 79:40-41). It is used for appetite, but also for opinion held out of preference, which is why the early scholars called sects the people of desires. The test is what you do when the proof turns out to go against what you wanted.

also written Hawaa · Hava · Ahwa · Ahwaa · Ahl al-ahwa · Desire

see also

The Prophet's pool, where his community drinks before entering Paradise and never thirsts again.

The narrations about it are numerous and agreed upon: its water whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, its cups like the stars of the sky. The Prophet peace be upon him said he will be at it ahead of his community, and that some who belonged to him will be turned away for what they introduced after him. Al-Kawthar, the river given to him in Paradise (Qur'an 108:1), is described in the reports as feeding it.

also written Haud · Hawdh · Hodh · Hawd al-Kawthar · Al-Kawthar · Kawthar

see also

The full lunar year that wealth must be held above the nisab before zakat falls due on it.

You set a date, usually a day in Ramadan for ease of memory, and pay on whatever qualifying wealth you hold on that date each year. Hanafis fold money that comes and goes during the year into that one date; the other schools start a fresh year for wealth newly acquired. Crops are the exception: their zakat is due at harvest, and buried treasure is due at once.

also written Haul · Hol · Howl · zakat year · lunar year for zakat · Hawl al-zakat

see also

A modesty that makes a person shrink from what is ugly, before Allah and before people.

The Prophet peace be upon him said modesty is a branch of faith, in Bukhari and Muslim, and that modesty brings nothing but good, in Muslim. It is a restraint that works before the act rather than a regret afterwards. It is not shyness of speech: a person can be modest and still ask a direct question, and the women of the Ansar were praised because shyness did not stop them learning their religion.

also written Haya · Hayaa · Haia · Hayaa' · Haja · Modesty

see also

Menstruation, during which prayer and fasting are lifted and intimacy is paused.

Prayers missed in these days are not made up, but fasts of Ramadan are. Nifas is the parallel state of bleeding after childbirth and carries the same rulings. Bleeding outside these two, called istihadah, does not excuse prayer or fasting. The schools differ over the minimum and maximum days of hayd, which changes when a woman resumes worship, so local guidance matters here.

also written Haid · Haiz · Hayz · Haydh · Hayd period · menstruation

see also

Memorising the Qur'an by heart, traditionally with a teacher who hears you every day.

The word means preservation, the same word the Qur'an uses when it says Allah has taken the preservation of this revelation upon Himself. Memorisation has been the main way that happened: in every generation enough people carried the whole text that no copy could quietly go missing. A memoriser adds a small portion each day and spends far more time revising than adding.

also written Hifdh · Hifdz · Hefz · Hifz Quran · Hifzul Quran · Tahfiz

see also

The covering a Muslim woman wears in public, most often a headscarf with modest clothing.

The command to draw the khimar over the neckline stands in Surah al-Nur, directly after the command to believing men to lower their gaze; the outer garment, the jilbab, is in Surah al-Ahzab. The word itself means a screen or curtain, and in the Qur'an it usually means a barrier rather than a garment; the everyday sense of headscarf is later usage. The schools agree on covering the hair and body and differ over the face and hands.

also written Hijaab · Hejab · Hicab · Purdah · Parda · Khimar

see also

Cupping: suction on the skin with small incisions to draw blood out, practised and praised by the Prophet.

He was cupped, peace be upon him, and said that among the best of the remedies people use is cupping, in reports collected by Bukhari and Muslim. It is a recommended treatment, not an act of worship and not a cure for everything, and the reports naming particular days of the month are weighed differently by different scholars. It should be done by someone trained and clean. It is medicine, and the ordinary rules of medicine apply to it.

also written Hijamah · Hejama · Hajama · Hijaama · Cupping · Wet cupping

see also

The low semicircular wall beside the Ka'bah, enclosing ground that is part of the original house.

When Quraysh rebuilt the Ka'bah they ran short of lawful money and left this stretch outside the walls. The Prophet told Aishah that if her people were not so new to Islam he would rebuild it on Ibrahim's foundation and bring the Hijr back inside. So praying in it counts as praying inside the Ka'bah, and this is also why tawaf must be made outside the wall, not between it and the building.

also written Hijr Ismail · Hateem · Al-Hatim · Hatim · Hijr · Hijir Ismail

see also

The Prophet's migration from Makkah to Madinah in 622, the start of the Muslim calendar.

The word means to leave something behind and cut ties with it. He left with Abu Bakr, hid three nights in the cave of Thawr while Quraysh searched, and reached Madinah to build a mosque and a community that could finally live its faith openly. Umar later chose this event, not the Prophet's birth or the first revelation, as year one, because it was the moment the community became a community. The Prophet also said the true muhajir is the one who leaves what Allah forbade.

also written Hijra · Hegira · Hijrat · Hijri · Hejira · Hijrah to Madinah

see also

The first migration, when persecuted Muslims fled Makkah to a Christian king in Abyssinia.

It happened in two waves, years before the move to Madinah. The Prophet sent them to the Negus, whom he described as a king under whom nobody is wronged. Quraysh sent envoys with gifts to demand them back; Ja'far ibn Abi Talib answered by describing what they had been and what Islam made of them, then recited from Surah Maryam, and the king wept and refused to hand them over. Some stayed until after Khaybar.

also written Hijrah Habashah · Migration to Abyssinia · Abyssinia · Habasha · Al-Habashah · Najashi

see also

The Muslim lunar calendar, counting years from the Hijrah and running about eleven days shorter than the solar year.

Umar established it, choosing the Hijrah as year one rather than the Prophet's birth or the first revelation. Its twelve months are Muharram, Safar, Rabi al-Awwal, Rabi ath-Thani, Jumada al-Ula, Jumada al-Akhirah, Rajab, Sha'ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul Qa'dah and Dhul Hijjah, and four of them are sacred. Because it is purely lunar, Ramadan and hajj move through all the seasons over roughly thirty three years, so every generation fasts both the long days and the short ones.

also written Hijri · Hijri year · AH · Islamic calendar · Lunar calendar · Taqwim Hijri

see also

Forbearance: the strength to stay calm and unhurried when you have every right to react.

The Prophet peace be upon him told al-Ashajj of Abd al-Qays that he had two qualities Allah loves, hilm and unhurriedness, in Muslim. The Qur'an describes the answer to a rough word as repelling with what is better (Qur'an 41:34). Hilm is not weakness and it is not indifference. The person is fully able to strike back and takes the slower road.

also written Hilim · Halim · Haleem · Hilm wa anah · Ana'ah · Anah

see also

The reckoning: each person shown their record and questioned about the life they were given.

The Qur'an describes books handed to the right hand and to the left, and an easy reckoning for some (Qur'an 84:7-9). The Prophet peace be upon him said that a servant's feet will not move on that Day until he is asked about his life, his knowledge, his wealth and his body, in a report collected by al-Tirmidhi. Sound narrations also describe a group entering Paradise with no reckoning at all.

also written Hisaab · Hesab · Hisab e Amal · Yawm al-Hisab · Reckoning · The Accounting
