A devil: any rebellious jinn, and with the definite article, Iblis himself.

The Qur'an says he is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy (Qur'an 35:6), and gives him only two tools, whispering and inviting. He cannot compel anyone; on the Day of Judgement he tells his own followers that he had no authority over them except that he called and they answered (Qur'an 14:22). The Qur'an also calls some human beings shayatin, so the word is not limited to jinn.

also written Shaitan · Shaytaan · Shaitaan · Sheytan · Sheitan · Syaitan

see also

The Makkan valley where the Prophet's clan was penned by a boycott for about three years.

Quraysh hung a written pact in the Ka'bah agreeing to no trade and no marriage with Banu Hashim until they surrendered him. Believer and unbeliever of the clan were shut in together, living on what sympathisers smuggled past the guards, and children's crying could be heard outside. It broke when several Quraysh who had never been comfortable with it tore the document up. Khadijah and Abu Talib both died soon after, in what is called the Year of Sorrow.

also written Shib Abi Talib · Shiab Abi Talib · Valley of Abu Talib · The Boycott · Social boycott of Banu Hashim · Shi'b Bani Hashim

see also

Giving to something other than Allah what belongs to Allah alone, above all worship.

The word means to make a partner or to share. The Qur'an says Allah does not forgive that a partner be set up with Him, and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills (Qur'an 4:48). Commentators read that of the one who dies without repenting, since the Qur'an elsewhere promises forgiveness to whoever turns back. Scholars distinguish major shirk, which takes a person outside Islam, from minor shirk, which is a grave sin but does not.

also written Shrik · Sherk · Shirek · Schirk · Associating partners with God · Polytheism

see also

Minor shirk: acts like showing off in worship, which damage sincerity without putting a person outside Islam.

The Prophet peace be upon him called showing off the lesser shirk, in a report collected by Imam Ahmad. Swearing by other than Allah, and saying what Allah and so and so willed, belong to the same family. The point is not to make a believer anxious about every sentence, but to keep worship pointed in one direction.

also written Minor shirk · Lesser shirk · Shirk al-Asghar · Shirk khafi · Hidden shirk · Riya

see also

Doubtful matters: the grey band between what is clearly lawful and what is clearly forbidden.

The Prophet peace be upon him said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are unclear matters that many people do not know, and whoever guards against them has protected his religion and his honour, in Bukhari and Muslim. The same hadith ends by naming the heart as the organ that settles the body. Leaving the doubtful is wara', and it is personal caution rather than a ruling you impose on other people.

also written Shubuhaat · Shubha · Shubhat · Mushtabihat · Doubtful matters · Grey area

see also

Gratitude that shows: knowing the gift, saying so, and using it as its Giver would like.

The Qur'an promises increase to those who are grateful (Qur'an 14:7). Scholars describe shukr working in three places at once: the heart admits where the gift came from, the tongue says it, and the limbs do not use the gift against the One who gave it. The Prophet peace be upon him also said that whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi.

also written Shukur · Shukran · Sukur · Shukr Allah · Shakir · Gratitude

see also

Truthfulness: that your words, your intentions and your actions all report the same thing.

The Qur'an tells the believers to be with the truthful (Qur'an 9:119), and the Prophet peace be upon him said truthfulness leads to righteousness and righteousness leads to Paradise, in Bukhari and Muslim. Writers on the heart use sidq more widely than honest speech: a truthful hope, a truthful repentance, a truthful claim to love Allah. In that sense its opposite is not only lying but posing.

also written Sedq · Sidk · Sidiq · Siddiq · Sadiq · Truthfulness

see also

The Lote Tree at the furthest limit, reached by the Prophet on the Night Journey.

The Qur'an says he saw him at a second descent, by the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge (Qur'an 53:13-15). Scholars describe it as the boundary past which the knowledge of creation does not go, so it marks a limit rather than a location. It appears in the accounts of the Night Journey, at the stage where the five daily prayers were given.

also written Sidratul Muntaha · Sidra tul Muntaha · Sidrat ul Muntaha · Sidratul Muntahaa · Sidrah · Lote Tree

see also

The qualities of each letter: whispered or voiced, heavy or light, tense or flowing.

Two letters can share one articulation point and still be different letters because their qualities differ, as with ta and da. Some qualities come in opposite pairs and some stand alone, like the whistle of sin or the roll of ra. Together with the makharij they are the two halves of pronouncing a letter correctly.

also written Sifat · Sifaat · Sifat al huruf · Sifaat ul huroof · Hams · Jahr

see also

Sorcery: real in its effect, but powerless to harm anyone except by Allah's permission.

The word covers sorcery worked with the help of devils, and the Qur'an describes it plainly while making clear that it harms nobody except by Allah's permission (Qur'an 2:102). The Prophet peace be upon him was himself affected by it, in Bukhari and Muslim, and he recovered; he also named it among the seven destructive sins. Learning it or commissioning it is a grave matter, and the schools of law differ over the penalty for the one who practises it. The treatment is ruqya, the daily adhkar and ordinary medicine, never counter-magic.

also written Sehr · Sihir · Sahir · Sehir · Magic · Black magic

see also

The life story of the Prophet Muhammad, told in order, from birth to death.

The root means to travel, so a sirah is the road a person walked. The oldest surviving account is Ibn Ishaq's, preserved in the edition of Ibn Hisham, alongside al-Waqidi and the Tabaqat of Ibn Sa'd. Sirah writers accepted material on a looser standard of proof than the hadith scholars did, so a story being famous in the sirah does not by itself make it authentic.

also written Seerah · Sira · Seera · Siera · Sirah Nabawiyyah · Seerat

see also

The bridge laid over Hell that everyone must cross, at speeds matching their deeds.

It is described in the long hadith of intercession in Bukhari and Muslim: people pass over it like lightning, like the wind, like a running horse, or crawling, and some are seized along the way. The Qur'an speaks of every one of you coming to it (Qur'an 19:71), which many commentators read as this crossing. The same word in Surah al-Fatihah means the straight path in this life, a different sense of one root.

also written Siraat · Sirath · Sarat · As-Sirat · Pul Sirat · Pul-e-Sirat

see also

A twig used to clean the teeth, recommended before prayer, wudu, and on waking.

It is cut from the arak tree, softened at one end into bristles. The Prophet said that were it not a hardship, he would have ordered it before every prayer. It is a sunnah of cleanliness rather than a condition of anything, and a toothbrush achieves most of the same purpose for anyone who has no arak wood.

also written Miswak · Meswak · Siwaak · Misvak · Arak stick · Salvadora persica

see also

Companionship: the people you sit with, treated in the sources as a cause of what you become.

The Prophet peace be upon him compared a good companion to a seller of musk and a bad one to a blacksmith's bellows, in Bukhari and Muslim, and said a person follows the way of his close friend, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Writers on the heart therefore treat the choice of company as an act with consequences rather than an accident. In Sufi usage suhbah also names the particular bond between a student and a teacher.

also written Suhba · Sohbet · Suhbat · Sohbat · Jalis · Companionship

see also

The meal eaten before dawn to begin a day of fasting.

The name comes from sahar, the last darkness before dawn. The Prophet said to eat it because there is blessing in it, and encouraged delaying it until close to the dawn. It is a sunnah rather than a condition, so a fast is still valid if a person sleeps through it.

also written Sehri · Sahur · Suhoor · Sohour · Sahri · Sehri time

see also

The prostration, forehead and nose on the ground, done twice in every rak'ah.

Seven parts touch the ground: the forehead with the nose, the two palms, the two knees, and the toes of both feet. The Prophet said a servant is nearest to his Lord in sujud, and told us to make much supplication there. It is the posture the whole prayer is built around, not a formality between recitations.

also written Sujood · Sajda · Sajdah · Sujuud · Sadjah · Sajood

see also

Two extra prostrations that repair a mistake made by forgetting during the prayer.

They cover adding a posture, leaving out a required part, or losing count. The Prophet said that when a person is unsure, he should settle on the lower number and make the two prostrations. The schools place them differently, before or after the closing salam depending on the kind of mistake, so follow what your local imam does rather than assuming an error.

also written Sujud as-sahw · Sajda sahw · Sajdah sahw · Sujood sahw · prostration of forgetfulness · Sahw

see also

A single prostration made when reciting or hearing one of the Qur'an's verses of prostration.

Copies of the Qur'an mark these verses in the margin. Depending on the school they are counted as eleven, fourteen or fifteen. It is one prostration, done inside or outside prayer, and it is recommended rather than required for most scholars. A related act is sujud ash-shukr, a prostration of thanks on receiving good news.

also written Sajdah tilawah · Sujood tilawah · Sajda e tilawat · prostration of recitation · Tilawah sajda · recitation prostration

see also

A hadith book arranged by the chapters of fiqh, gathering the reports a jurist needs.

The four Sunan among the six books are those of Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and in its own way al-Tirmidhi. Unlike the two Sahihs they include weak reports, usually with a remark, because their purpose is to lay out the evidence on each legal question rather than to collect only what is sound. Reading them well means reading the author's comments, not only the texts.

also written Sunen · As-Sunan · Sunan books · Sunan Abi Dawud · Sunan Abu Dawood · Sunan al-Nasai

see also

The Prophet's way in belief, worship and conduct, and the measure against which innovation is judged.

The word means a trodden path. In hadith study it covers what the Prophet peace be upon him said, did, and quietly approved; in fiqh it also names a recommended act; in creed it means the received way of the first generations, which is why the phrase Ahl al-Sunnah exists. Set against bid'ah, sunnah means the shape of the religion as it was handed over, rather than anyone's personal preference.

also written Sunna · Sunnat · As-Sunnah · Sunnahs · Sunan · Way of the Prophet

see also

The regular voluntary prayers attached before or after the five obligatory ones.

Twelve rak'ahs are reported as the standing pattern: two before Fajr, four before and two after Dhuhr, two after Maghrib, and two after Isha. The two before Fajr were the ones the Prophet never left. Any voluntary prayer outside this pattern is called nafl, and it carries no blame if missed.

also written Sunan rawatib · Rawatib · Ratibah · Sunnah muakkadah · Sunnat · Sunnah prayers

see also

The horn that is blown to end this world, and blown again to raise the dead.

The Qur'an says the horn is blown and everyone in the heavens and the earth falls dead except whom Allah wills, then it is blown a second time and they are standing, looking on (Qur'an 39:68). The angel entrusted with it is named Israfil in the hadith literature. Reports describe him holding it to his mouth, head inclined, waiting for the command.

also written Soor · Sour · As-Sur · Nafkh as-Sur · The Trumpet · The Horn

see also

A chapter of the Qur'an; there are 114, arranged in the mushaf rather than by date of revelation.

Each surah has a name, usually taken from a striking word inside it, and every surah except at-Tawbah opens with the basmalah. They range from al-Baqarah at 286 verses down to al-Kawthar at three. The order in the mushaf is not the order of revelation, so many of the short surahs at the end are among the earliest to come down.

also written Sura · Soorah · Surat · Suratul · Suwar · Sourate

see also

T

Interpretation, and in a second sense the reality a statement finally turns out to refer to.

Early scholars used ta'wil and tafsir almost interchangeably; Tabari's great commentary carries the word in its title. Later it came to mean moving a word away from its apparent sense on the strength of evidence, which is where much theological argument lives. In Shia and Sufi writing the word often carries a further sense, an inner meaning beneath the plain one, which Sunni scholars accept only where it does not cancel the plain meaning.

also written Tawil · Ta'weel · Taweel · Taawil · Tavil · Batin

see also

Discretionary punishment, set by a judge for offences that carry no fixed penalty.

The word means correction. It covers the vast majority of wrongdoing, from fraud and bribery to public nuisance, and it can be a warning, a fine, imprisonment or public rebuke. The judge weighs the person, the offence and the circumstances, and most jurists hold that ta'zir must stay below the level of a hadd. This flexible category, and not the hudud, is where classical Islamic criminal justice actually did its daily work.

also written Tazir · Taazir · Tazirat · Tazeer · Taazeer · Tezir

see also

Seeking blessing through a person, place or object, which scholars permit narrowly and dispute widely.

The Companions sought blessing through the person of the Prophet peace be upon him, his hair and the water left from his wudu, which is established in Bukhari and Muslim. Everyone agrees that the blessing itself comes from Allah alone. Scholars disagree about extending the practice after his death to graves, relics and living righteous people, some permitting it within limits, others treating it as a door that opens onto shirk. All sides agree that asking the object itself for anything is not tabarruk but worship of it.

also written Tabaruk · Tabaruck · Tabarruk bil-athar · Seeking blessing · Barakah from relics · Relics

see also

The third generation: those who met the Followers, the last age the Prophet praised by name.

Malik ibn Anas, Sufyan ath-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Shu'bah and Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak stand in this layer. It is the generation in which the schools of law took shape and hadith began to be gathered into books rather than carried in memory alone. Together with the Companions and the Followers they make up the salaf, the three generations of praise.

also written Tabi at-Tabiin · Taba Tabieen · Atba at-Tabiin · Atbaa ut Tabieen · Tabe Tabaeen · Third generation

see also

A Muslim of the generation after the Companions, who met a Companion but not the Prophet.

The plural is tabi'un or tabi'in. They form the second layer in almost every chain, and figures like Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibn Sirin belong here. Their own statements are called maqtu', and their reports about the Prophet without naming the Companion in between are called mursal.

also written Tabii · Tabi · Tabi'in · Tabiin · Tabi'een · Tabieen

see also

The second generation: Muslims who met Companions but never met the Prophet himself.

They are the ones who received Islam warm from the hands that had held it, and they built the first schools of law and Qur'an teaching. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Sirin and Urwah ibn az-Zubayr belong here, and the Prophet named Uways al-Qarani the best of them without ever meeting him. The Prophet said the best of people are his generation, then those who follow them, then those who follow them.

also written Tabiun · Tabieen · Tabi'in · Tabiin · Tabaeen · Taabieen

see also

The last expedition the Prophet led, a long march north in year nine that ended without battle.

It was called the army of hardship: high summer, scarce water, ripe harvests left behind, and a distant enemy. Uthman equipped a large part of it from his own wealth. No fighting took place. Its lasting story is the three Companions who simply failed to go and would not lie about why; the community was told to shun them for fifty nights until Surah at-Tawbah announced that Allah had turned to them, a passage that is really about honesty when a lie would have been easy.

also written Battle of Tabuk · Ghazwat Tabuk · Jaysh al-Usrah · Army of Hardship · Tabook · Tebuk

see also

Slow reflection on the Qur'an, letting a verse work on you instead of passing over it.

The root means to look at the far end of a thing, to follow it to its outcome. The Qur'an names this as the purpose of its revelation and asks more than once whether people reflect on it at all. Tadabbur is not tafsir: it needs no training, only attention, honesty, and enough of the meaning to know what you are reading.

also written Tadabur · Tadabbor · Tadabbur al-Quran · Tadabbur e Quran · reflection on the Quran · pondering the Quran

see also

Wording a chain so that a gap or a weak teacher is hidden, without stating an outright lie.

The word comes from trading in dim light so the buyer cannot see the flaw. The classic form is a narrator saying from so and so about a man he met but did not hear this particular report from. Scholars listed the known mudallisin in ranks, and as a rule they do not accept such a narrator's report unless he says plainly that he heard it.

also written Tadlees · Tedlis · Mudallis · Mudallas · Mudalis · Tadleese

see also

The middle speed of recitation, sitting between the slow tartil and the quick hadr.

It keeps every rule of tajwid fully in place while moving at a working pace. This is how most imams recite in tarawih and how most students revise. All three speeds are permitted; what is not permitted is speed that swallows letters.

also written Tadweer · Tadwer · Tadwir recitation · medium speed recitation · middle pace · Tadwir Quran

see also

Deliberate reflection on creation and on your own life, treated as an act of worship.

The Qur'an describes people of understanding as those who remember Allah standing, sitting and lying on their sides, and who reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth (Qur'an 3:190-191). Scholars direct tafakkur outward at what has been made, and inward at one's own conduct, rather than at the nature of Allah Himself, which the mind cannot hold. A short honest stretch of thinking counts for more than a long distracted one.

also written Tafakur · Tefekkur · Tafkir · Tafakkur fi khalq · Reflection · Contemplation

see also

Heavy and light pronunciation: some letters fill the mouth, others stay thin.

Seven letters are always heavy, gathered by teachers in a mnemonic phrase, khussa daghtin qiz. Ra and the lam in the name Allah switch between heavy and light depending on the vowels around them, and alif simply follows whatever came before it. The distinction is not decorative: a heavy letter said thin can turn one word into a different word.

also written Tafkhim · Tafkheem · Tarqiq · Tarqeeq · Tafkheem tarqeeq · Isti'la

see also

Explanation of the Qur'an: what a verse means, why it came, and what it asks of you.

The word means to uncover, the way you pull a cover off a thing. A tafsir works through the text verse by verse using the rest of the Qur'an, the Sunnah, the sayings of the Companions and the Arabic language. Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi are among the best known, and they differ in focus, so reading one is not reading them all.

also written Tafseer · Tefsir · Tafsear · Tafsire · Tafsirul Quran · Tafseer ul Quran

see also

Tafsir built on transmitted reports, as against tafsir bi'r-ra'y, which reasons from language and principle.

Transmitted tafsir explains the Qur'an by the Qur'an, then by the Sunnah, then by the Companions and their students. Reasoned tafsir uses grammar, context and legal principle; it is praised when it is disciplined and condemned when it is a person reading their preferences into the text. Most of the great commentaries mix the two rather than holding to one.

also written Tafsir bil Mathur · Tafsir bil-ma'thoor · Tafseer bil mathoor · Tafsir bir-ray · Tafsir bil ray · Tafsir bil rai

see also

Leaving the meaning of a difficult divine attribute to Allah, as opposed to interpreting it figuratively.

When the texts describe Allah with a hand, a face, or a rising, scholars took two broad roads. Tafwid affirms the word and consigns its reality to Allah without explaining it. Ta'wil interprets it within what the Arabic allows, such as hand meaning power. Atharis lean to the first and Ash'aris and Maturidis often to the second, and each counts the other as Sunni.

also written Tafweed · Tafwidh · Tafwiz · Consigning the meaning · Leaving the meaning to Allah · Bila kayf

see also

Voluntary prayer in the night, traditionally after sleeping and before dawn.

The root means to give up sleep. The Qur'an addresses the Prophet directly about it, and the last third of the night is its best time. There is no fixed number of rak'ahs; two is enough. Qiyam al-layl is a broader term for any prayer of the night, and in ordinary use the two words are treated as the same thing.

also written Tahajud · Tahujjud · Tahjud · Qiyam al-layl · Qiyamul layl · night prayer

see also

Coming out of ihram, so that what was forbidden during it becomes permitted again.

In hajj it happens in two stages. The first comes after stoning Jamrat al-Aqabah and cutting the hair: normal clothes and perfume return, but intimacy does not. The second comes after tawaf al-ifadah and its sa'i, and lifts everything. In umrah there is only one, after the hair is cut.

also written Tahalul · Tahallal · exiting ihram · leaving ihram · coming out of ihram · Tahallul awwal

see also

Ritual purity, the state a person must be in before praying and, for most scholars, before touching the Qur'an.

Books of fiqh almost always begin with taharah, because it is the gate to everything else. It has two sides: removing physical filth from the body, clothes and place of prayer, and lifting the ritual states that block worship. The Prophet called purification half of faith, and the Qur'an says Allah loves those who keep themselves pure.

also written Tahara · Tahaarah · Tahaarat · Taharat · Tuhur · purity

see also

The rules for pronouncing the Qur'an correctly: each letter from its place, with its proper qualities.

The word means to do a thing well. In practice it covers articulation points, letter qualities, lengthening, merging, hiding, and where to stop. Scholars broadly agree that learning enough to avoid errors that change meaning is required of every reciter; how much of the finer detail is obligatory is debated, and a beginner is not sinful for reciting imperfectly while learning.

also written Tajweed · Tadjwid · Tajvid · Tajwed · Tejwid · Tajweed rules

see also

Cooperative insurance, built on mutual donation, offered as an alternative to conventional policies.

Participants contribute to a shared fund on the basis of tabarru', donation, and the fund pays claims, while an operator manages it for a fee or an agreed share. It was designed to answer the objections scholars raise against conventional insurance, namely gharar, resemblance to gambling, and interest bearing reserves. Not every scholar accepts that the difference is substantive, and some hold conventional insurance permissible under necessity where no alternative is available.

also written Takafol · Takafful · Tekaful · Takaful insurance · Tabarru · Ta'awun

see also

The opening "Allahu akbar" that begins the prayer and closes off everything outside it.

Ihram here means entering a sanctified state, the same root as the pilgrim's ihram. Once you say the opening takbir, eating, speaking and turning away are no longer permitted until the closing salam. Smaller takbirs then mark each change of posture through the prayer.

also written Takbir · Takbeer · Allahu akbar · Takbiratul ihram · opening takbir · Takbira

see also

Declaring a specific Muslim to be a disbeliever, a ruling classical scholars fenced with heavy conditions.

Scholarship treats takfir as a judgement with conditions and impediments: ignorance, misreading, compulsion, and the absence of clear proof all block it. The Prophet peace be upon him warned that when a man calls his brother a disbeliever it returns to one of the two, in a report in Bukhari and Muslim. Saying that a statement is disbelief is not the same as saying the person who said it is a disbeliever, and the second was left to qualified scholars.

also written Takfeer · Takfiri · Takfeeri · Declaring someone a kafir · Excommunication · Calling someone a disbeliever

see also

Tracing a hadith to the books that recorded it, gathering its chains, and then grading it.

The work has three steps: find where it was narrated, collect every route it came by, and weigh them together. It is the step most often skipped when a hadith is quoted online. A proper takhrij gives the source and the verdict, so a reader can check the claim instead of trusting whoever is quoting it.

also written Takhreej · Tahrij · Takhrij al-hadith · Takhreej al-hadeeth · Tracing a hadith · Referencing hadith

see also

Divorce pronounced by the husband, which Islamic law permits but treats as a last resort.

The Qur'an gives it a whole surah and sets out a careful procedure: a single pronouncement, then a waiting period during which the couple may simply resume, with two further chances before the separation becomes final. Three pronouncements in one sitting are counted as three by the majority and as one by a minority, and this is among the oldest live disputes in fiqh. A woman who wishes to end a marriage uses khul' or asks a judge for faskh instead.

also written Talak · Talaaq · Tallaq · Talq · Talaqe · Triple talaq

see also

The pilgrim's answering call, beginning labbayk Allahumma labbayk, here I am, my Lord, here I am.

It continues: no partner have You, here I am, all praise and favour are Yours, and the dominion, You have no partner. It is said on entering ihram and repeated on the road, aloud by men and quietly by women. It is an answer to the summons the Qur'an says Ibrahim was told to proclaim. On umrah pilgrims stop when they begin the tawaf; on hajj the talbiyah continues until the stoning on the tenth.

also written Talbiya · Labbaik · Labbayk · Labbaik Allahumma labbaik · Talbeeyah · Telbiye

see also

One of the three ways to perform hajj: umrah first, then leaving ihram, then hajj from Makkah.

In tamattu' you complete umrah, come out of ihram and wait, then enter ihram again for hajj on the eighth. In qiran you hold both in a single unbroken ihram, and in ifrad you perform hajj alone. Tamattu' and qiran require a hady; ifrad does not. The schools differ over which is best, and tamattu' is what most pilgrims on organised trips perform.

also written Tamattu · Tamatu · Temettu · Qiran · Qiraan · Ifrad

see also

An amulet worn for protection, whose ruling depends on what has been put inside it.

Amulets containing the names of jinn, unknown words or symbols are forbidden by agreement, and the Prophet peace be upon him warned that whoever hangs an amulet has been left to it, in reports collected by Ahmad and Tirmidhi. Amulets containing Qur'an are where scholars part company: Ibn Mas'ud and many after him prohibited them without distinction, while Abdullah ibn Amr and a number of Malikis and Shafi'is allowed the Qur'anic kind. Both sides agree the protection is from Allah, not from the paper.

also written Tameemah · Tamima · Tamaim · Taweez · Tawiz · Ta'wiz

see also

Following a qualified scholar's ruling without knowing the underlying evidence yourself.

It is what most Muslims do most of the time, and the Qur'an tells those who do not know to ask those who do. Scholars differ over its limits: some hold a layperson should commit to one school for coherence, others allow asking any trustworthy scholar, and all agree taqlid is not followed against a clear text one actually knows. The word is also used critically, for copying without thought, which is a different matter from consulting an expert.

also written Taqleed · Taklid · Taqlead · Taqliid · Muqallid · following a scholar

see also

Trimming the hair rather than shaving it, the alternative way to leave ihram.

Most schools require a little to be taken from all around the head rather than a single snip from one place. It is the option chosen by women, and by men who wish to keep hair for a shave at the end of a hajj that follows soon after. Both halq and taqsir close the rites of umrah, and no further trimming is needed after that.

also written Taqseer · Taksir · Taqsir hair · trimming hair · cutting hair in umrah · Tasqir

see also

An alert, careful awareness of Allah that keeps a person away from what harms them.

The root means to guard or to shield, and carries the sense of putting something between yourself and danger. The Qur'an calls it the best provision for the journey (Qur'an 2:197), and the Prophet peace be upon him pointed to his chest three times and said taqwa is here, in a report collected by Muslim. It is not fear alone, and it is not a personality type. It is caution kept awake.

also written Taqwah · Takwa · Taqwaa · Taqua · Tuqa · Takva

see also

The night prayer of Ramadan, prayed in congregation after Isha through the month.

The name comes from the pauses for rest taken after every four rak'ahs. The number differs by custom and school: twenty rak'ahs became the settled practice of most schools and thirty six the old practice of Madinah, while many mosques pray eight, following reports of the Prophet's own night prayer. The number is not the point of the argument it is often made into; both are within the tradition.

also written Taraweeh · Tarawee · Taravih · Salat at-tarawih · Ramadan night prayer · Terawih

see also

A Sufi order: a lineage with a shaykh, a set litany, and a method for training students.

The word means path. Well known orders include the Qadiriyyah, the Naqshbandiyyah, the Shadhiliyyah and the Chishtiyyah, each with its own wird and manners. Belonging to one has never been a requirement in Islam, and scholars differ sharply about the orders as institutions, some treating them as a school of character, others objecting to particular practices found within them. The word is not used in this sense outside Sufi circles.

also written Tariqa · Tareeqa · Tarika · Tariqat · Turuq · Sufi order

see also

A translation of the Qur'an, properly called a translation of the meanings rather than the Qur'an itself.

No translation carries the Arabic wording, and every translator has already made interpretive choices, so a translation is really a compressed tafsir. This is why prayer is recited in Arabic; Abu Hanifah is reported to have allowed reciting the meaning in prayer, his two main students allowed it only for someone genuinely unable, and he is reported to have come round to their view. A translated volume is also not given the same rulings as a mushaf.

also written Tarjuma · Tarjama · Tarjumah · Tarjumatul Quran · translation of the Quran · Quran translation

see also

Reciting slowly and distinctly, giving every letter its right, as the Qur'an itself instructs.

The command is direct: and recite the Qur'an with tartil. Ali is reported to have explained it as giving the letters their due and knowing where to stop. It was the Prophet's own pace, and it is the one to use if you want to understand what you are saying.

also written Tarteel · Tartil Quran · Tarateel · Tartil recitation · slow recitation · measured recitation

see also

The Islamic tradition of inner purification, called Sufism in English, and read very differently by different scholars.

At its origin the word names the science of the heart: sincerity, remembrance, character and struggle against the self, as taught by early figures such as al-Junayd and later organised by al-Ghazali. Over the centuries it also grew orders, practices and claims that other scholars judged to be innovations, and opinion today runs from full acceptance to full rejection, with many holding the content sound wherever it stays inside the Book and the Sunnah. When you meet the word it helps to ask which is meant: the subject matter, or a particular order and what it does.

also written Tasawuf · Tassawuf · Tasavvuf · Soofism · Sufism · Sufi

see also

Declaring Allah free of every imperfection, most often in the words subhan Allah.

The Prophet peace be upon him said two phrases are light on the tongue and heavy on the scale, subhan Allah wa bihamdih and subhan Allah al-azim, in Bukhari and Muslim, and he taught the counts said before sleeping. He counted on his fingers and told the women to do the same, since the fingers will be asked to testify, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Counting with beads was not the practice of his time; most later scholars allowed it as a tool, while some regarded it as an unwarranted addition.

also written Tasbeeh · Tesbih · Tasbi · Tasbih Fatimah · Subhanallah · Subhan Allah

see also

The words said while sitting in prayer, testifying to faith and greeting the Prophet.

The name comes from shahadah, testimony, because the words contain the declaration of faith. It is said in the sitting after the second rak'ah and again at the end of the prayer, where salawat on the Prophet is added before the closing salam. Several wordings are authentically reported, and mosques in different regions use different ones; all of them are sound.

also written Tashahud · Tashhahud · At-tahiyyat · Attahiyat · Tahiyyat · Tahiyat

see also

Likening Allah to His creation, which the Qur'an rules out with the words: there is nothing like Him.

Tashbih is imagining Allah as a bigger, stronger version of something you have already seen. Its mirror error is ta'til, emptying His names and attributes of any real meaning. Sunni creed walks between the two: He is real, He is described, and He is not comparable (Qur'an 42:11).

also written Tashbeeh · Tajsim · Tamthil · Anthropomorphism · Likening God to creation · Tashbih wa Tajsim

see also

The closing greeting of peace, turned to the right then the left, that ends the prayer.

You say as-salamu alaykum wa rahmatullah while turning the face to the right shoulder, then repeat it to the left. Until the taslim you are still in prayer and its restrictions apply. Some schools treat only the first salam as obligatory and the second as recommended.

also written Tasleem · Salam · Salaam · Assalamu alaykum in prayer · ending the prayer · Taslim in salah

see also

Humility: knowing your size, without pretending to be smaller than you are.

The Prophet peace be upon him said nobody humbles himself for Allah except that Allah raises him, in Muslim, and the Qur'an describes the servants of the Most Merciful as those who walk on the earth gently (Qur'an 25:63). Scholars define it as accepting the truth from whoever brings it, and not seeing yourself as above anyone. Performed modesty, staged so that people will admire it, belongs with riya rather than with tawadu'.

also written Tawaduh · Tawadhu · Tawaduu · Tevazu · Tawadhu' · Humility

see also

Circling the Kaaba seven times, keeping it on your left, starting and ending at the Black Stone.

The Qur'an commands circling the Ancient House. Most schools require the pilgrim to be in a state of purity, and Hanafis count a tawaf made without wudu as valid but owing a dam. Each circuit begins and ends at the corner of the Black Stone. Hajj has up to three: tawaf al-qudum on arrival, tawaf al-ifadah after Arafah which is a pillar of the hajj, and tawaf al-wada as a farewell before leaving Makkah. There is no obligation to touch or kiss the stone; most pilgrims simply point to it.

also written Tawaaf · Tawwaf · Tavaf · Tauf · circumambulation · circling the Kaaba

see also

Relying on Allah for the outcome while still doing the work that leads to it.

The Qur'an says whoever relies on Allah, He is enough for him (Qur'an 65:3), and it also tells the Prophet peace be upon him to consult, then decide, then rely (Qur'an 3:159). When a man asked whether to leave his camel loose and trust Allah, he was told to tie it and then trust, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Tawakkul is the state of the heart after you have done what you can, not a reason to do nothing.

also written Tawakul · Tawakkal · Tawaqul · Tevekkul · Tawakkul alallah · Reliance on Allah

see also

Approaching Allah through a means, such as His names, your own good deeds, or a living person's du'a.

All schools agree on three forms: by Allah's names and attributes, by your own righteous deeds, and by asking a living righteous person to pray for you, the last shown in the hadith of the blind man and in Umar asking al-Abbas to pray for rain. They differ over tawassul by the person or rank of a prophet or saint, especially after death. Many Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Sufi scholars permit it as a form of asking Allah, while Hanbali and Salafi scholarship generally rejects it as a door to worse. All sides agree that asking the dead to grant something themselves is not tawassul at all but shirk.

also written Tawasul · Tawassal · Tawwasul · Tawassul bil anbiya · Seeking a means · Intermediary

see also

Turning back to Allah from a sin: stopping it, regretting it, and resolving not to return.

The Qur'an calls for a sincere turning, tawbatan nasuha (Qur'an 66:8). Scholars list the conditions as leaving the sin, regretting it, resolving not to repeat it, and, where a person's right was taken, returning it or seeking their pardon. The Prophet peace be upon him said every child of Adam errs, and the best of those who err are those who repent, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Falling again does not cancel the earlier repentance; it calls for another one.

also written Tawba · Tauba · Taubah · Touba · Tobah · Tawbah nasuha

see also

The belief that Allah is one, without partner, without equal, and alone deserving of worship.

The word means to make one, or to declare one. Surah al-Ikhlas states it in four short lines: He is One, the Eternal Refuge, He does not beget and was not begotten, and there is nothing comparable to Him (Qur'an 112). Tawhid is not only the claim that one God exists. It is that only He is worshipped.

also written Tawheed · Tauhid · Towhid · Tevhid · Tawhiid · Tauheed

see also

Oneness of lordship: that Allah alone creates, owns, sustains and controls everything that exists.

This is the belief that there is one Creator running one universe, and the Qur'an notes that even the idolaters of Makkah admitted this much when asked who made the heavens and the earth. That is why it is not, by itself, enough to make someone a Muslim. The three part division of tawhid is a teaching framework, used widely since Ibn Taymiyyah; some scholars prefer a two part arrangement, and the difference is about how to teach it rather than what is true.

also written Rububiyyah · Ruboobiyyah · Rububiya · Tawheed ar-Rububiyyah · Tawhid Rububiyya · Oneness of Lordship

see also

Oneness of worship: that prayer, vows, sacrifice, hope and fear are directed to Allah alone.

This is the part the messengers were sent with, and the part people have always argued over. To believe Allah made you is one thing; to bring every act of worship to Him and to no one else is another. Its exact opposite is shirk.

also written Uluhiyyah · Uloohiyyah · Ilahiyyah · Tawhid al-Ibadah · Tawheed al-Uluhiyyah · Oneness of worship

see also

Purification with clean earth instead of water, when water is unavailable or would cause harm.

You strike clean ground or dust with the palms and wipe the face and the hands. The Qur'an permits it for the traveller, the ill, and anyone who cannot find water. It stands in for both wudu and ghusl, and it ends the moment water becomes usable again. It is a real concession, not a lesser or shameful substitute.

also written Tayamum · Tayammom · Teyemmum · Tayammun · dry ablution · dry wudu

see also

The purification of the self: the work of clearing the heart of what spoils it.

The Qur'an says the one who purifies the soul has succeeded (Qur'an 91:9), and lists purifying people among the tasks the Prophet peace be upon him was sent with (Qur'an 62:2). The subject covers both halves of the job: removing what is blameworthy, such as envy and arrogance, and planting what is praiseworthy, such as sincerity and gratitude. It is a discipline with a syllabus, not a mood, and it belongs to every Muslim rather than to one group.

also written Tazkiya · Tazkiah · Tazkiyat al-nafs · Tazkiyah al-nafs · Tazkiat · Tazkiyya

see also

A trustworthy narrator: upright in character and accurate in memory, the two conditions held together.

Uprightness without accuracy gives you a sincere man who misremembers. Accuracy without uprightness gives you a sharp man who lies. Only both together make a thiqah. Ranks below it include saduq, meaning truthful but slightly less precise, and layyin, meaning soft or weak.

also written Thiqa · Siqah · Siqa · Tiqah · Thiqaat · Thiqat

see also

Reciting the Qur'an aloud, following its words closely rather than merely reading over them.

The root carries the sense of following, one word behind another, which is why the term implies obedience as well as recitation. The Qur'an praises those who recite it as it deserves to be recited. In practice tilawah is done with wudu where possible, at a measured pace, opening with the isti'adhah.

also written Tilawa · Tilaawah · Tilawat · Telawa · Tilawah Quran · Tilawat e Quran

see also

Whether wudu is needed to hold a copy of the Qur'an; the four schools say yes, a minority disagrees.

The four Sunni schools require purity to touch the mushaf itself, citing a verse in Surah al-Waqi'ah and the Prophet's letter to the people of Yemen; Ibn Hazm and others read that verse as speaking about the angels instead. Reciting from memory without wudu is agreed to be fine. Most contemporary scholars hold that a phone or tablet is not a mushaf, so the ruling does not extend to reading from a screen.

also written Mass al-Mushaf · Massul Mushaf · touching the Quran · touching Quran without wudu · holding the Quran · Quran without ablution

see also

The beginner's tajwid poem students memorise, alongside al-Jazariyyah and, for the readings, ash-Shatibiyyah.

Tuhfat al-Atfal, by al-Jamzuri, covers the rules of nun sakinah, meem sakinah and madd in about sixty lines of verse. Al-Jazariyyah, by Ibn al-Jazari, goes further into the articulation points and qualities of the letters. Ash-Shatibiyyah is the long poem behind the seven readings, and students normally reach it only after the first two are secure.

also written Tuhfatul Atfal · Tuhfa · Tohfatul Atfal · Jazariyyah · Al-Jazariyyah · Muqaddimah al-Jazariyyah

see also

U

The animal sacrificed on Eid al-Adha and the days after it, in remembrance of Ibrahim.

It is offered after the Eid prayer on the tenth of Dhul Hijjah and through the days of tashriq. The Hanafis hold it obligatory on whoever has the means; the other three schools call it a confirmed sunnah. The meat is customarily divided in three, for the household, for relatives and neighbours, and for the poor, though that division is a practice rather than a fixed ruling. It is not the same as the hady, the sacrifice a pilgrim offers as part of Hajj.

also written Qurbani · Qurban · Korban · Kurban · Adahi · Dhabihah of Eid

see also

The battle at the mountain outside Madinah where an early Muslim advantage collapsed into losses.

The Prophet posted archers on a hill and told them not to leave it whatever happened. When Quraysh broke and the Muslims began collecting spoils, most of the archers came down, and Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry came round the open flank. Around seventy Companions were killed, including Hamzah, and the Prophet himself was wounded. Surah Al Imran discusses the day at length, without softening it, which is part of why the Qur'an's honesty about its own community is striking.

also written Battle of Uhud · Ghazwat Uhud · Jang e Uhud · Ohod · Uhad · Mount Uhud

see also

The science of testing reports about the Prophet, deciding which are sound and which are not.

Every report is judged from two sides: the chain of people who passed it on, and the wording they carried. The classic handbook is the Muqaddimah of Ibn al-Salah, and Ibn Hajar's short Nukhbat al-Fikar is the summary students still memorise.

also written Uloom al-Hadith · Ilm al-Hadith · Mustalah al-Hadith · Mustalah · Hadith sciences · Ulum ul Hadith

see also

The family of disciplines that study how the Qur'an was revealed, collected, recited, read and interpreted.

It covers revelation and its occasions, Makkan and Madinan passages, the canonical readings, abrogation, the clear and the ambiguous, and the rules of interpretation. It is the map you are meant to have before opening a work of tafsir. The two classic reference works are al-Zarkashi's al-Burhan and al-Suyuti's al-Itqan.

also written Uloom al-Quran · Ulum ul Quran · Ulumul Quran · Uloom ul Quran · Quranic sciences · sciences of the Quran

see also

The Umayyad caliph whose short reign is remembered as a return to the way of the Rashidun.

He ruled about two and a half years from the ninety ninth year of the Hijrah. He returned property his family had taken, stopped the cursing of Ali from the pulpits, lightened taxes on new Muslims, and lived so plainly that his own household noticed the change first. He is also the caliph who ordered hadith to be gathered and written down systematically, which is why so much survives. Many scholars call him the fifth of the rightly guided caliphs.

also written Umar bin Abdul Aziz · Omar ibn Abdul Aziz · Umar II · Omar bin Abdulaziz · Umar ibn Abdulaziz · Fifth rightly guided caliph

see also

The second caliph, called al-Faruq, under whom the Muslim state expanded enormously.

He had set out to kill the Prophet and accepted Islam on the road, after hearing Surah Ta Ha in his sister's house. As caliph for about ten years he took Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia, and built the machinery of a state: a treasury, a stipend register, provincial governors held to account, and the Hijri calendar. Several rulings were revealed in line with opinions he had voiced. He walked Madinah at night without guards, and was stabbed while leading fajr.

also written Umar · Omar · Umar bin Khattab · Umar al-Faruq · Omar ibn al-Khattab · Hazrat Umar

see also

The whole body of Muslims, across every land and century, treated as one community.

The root is umm, mother, so an ummah is a people gathered around one origin. The Qur'an calls this community a middle nation and says your ummah is one ummah, and it uses the same word for other nations, for a stretch of time, and once for Ibrahim alone, a single man called a whole community. In practice the word carries a duty: what happens to Muslims elsewhere is not other people's news.

also written Umma · Ummat · Ummah Muslimah · Umat · Oomah · Ummet

see also

The Prophet's wives, whom the Qur'an names as mothers to every believer.

Surah al-Ahzab says his wives are their mothers, and in the same surah forbids anyone to marry them after him. He was married to eleven women across his life, nine of whom survived him; for twenty five years, until he was fifty, he was married to Khadijah alone. Several were widows, and the marriages knitted together tribes that had been enemies. Aishah and Umm Salamah in particular transmitted a large part of what is known about his private practice.

also written Ummahat ul Muminin · Ummahatul Mumineen · Mothers of the Believers · Ummahat al-Mumineen · Ummuhat al-Muminin · Wives of the Prophet

see also

The lesser pilgrimage: ihram, tawaf, sa'i and cutting the hair, and it may be done any time of year.

It shares its rites with hajj but has no Arafah, no Mina and no fixed date. It takes a few hours rather than several days. Shafi'is and Hanbalis hold umrah obligatory once in a lifetime; Hanafis and Malikis call it a confirmed sunnah. Performing it in Ramadan is described in a well known hadith as equal in reward to a hajj, which does not remove the obligation of hajj itself.

also written Umra · Omra · Umrah pilgrimage · Umre · lesser pilgrimage · minor pilgrimage

see also

The science of how rulings are derived: which sources count, and how they are read.

Literally the roots of fiqh. Where fiqh gives you the answer, usul al-fiqh gives you the method: the four sources agreed by the Sunni schools are the Qur'an, the Sunnah, ijma' and qiyas, together with rules for language, abrogation and conflicting evidence. Al-Shafi'i's Risalah is the earliest surviving book devoted to the subject.

also written Usul al fiqh · Usool al-Fiqh · Usul ul Fiqh · Usul fiqh · Osul al-Fiqh · Usul

see also

The third caliph, called Dhun-Nurayn, who fixed the Qur'an in one agreed written text.

The title means possessor of two lights, because he married two of the Prophet's daughters in turn. He was wealthy and gave heavily: he bought the well of Rumah for the people of Madinah and equipped much of the army of Tabuk. His great act as caliph was to standardise the mushaf, sending official copies to the provinces when he saw reciters disputing over readings. Rebels besieged his house and killed him while he was reading the Qur'an; he refused to let anyone fight for him.

also written Uthman · Usman · Osman · Othman · Uthman bin Affan · Hazrat Usman

see also

W

Revelation: Allah's speech conveyed to a prophet, directly, from behind a veil, or through an angel.

The Qur'an describes exactly those three modes (Qur'an 42:51), and says the Prophet peace be upon him did not speak from desire, but that it was revelation revealed (Qur'an 53:3-4). Revelation of this kind came to prophets only, and it ended with the death of the last of them. Nothing after him, however sincere or however true it feels, carries the same authority. Where the Qur'an uses the same verb of the bee or of the mother of Musa, scholars read inspiration rather than prophecy.

also written Wahi · Wahee · Wahyi · Vahiy · Wahyu · Revelation

see also

Obligatory. In the Hanafi school, a step below fard, resting on slightly weaker evidence.

For Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis, wajib and fard are two words for one category. Hanafis separate them: the witr prayer and the sacrifice at Eid al-Adha are wajib rather than fard, so neglecting them is sinful while denying them is not disbelief. In hajj the distinction has a practical edge, since a missed wajib can be repaired by a sacrifice while a missed pillar cannot.

also written Waajib · Wajeb · Vacip · Vajib · Wujub · Wajibat

see also

The male relative who contracts a woman's marriage on her behalf, usually her father.

Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis hold a marriage invalid without one, citing the report that there is no marriage without a wali. Hanafis hold that an adult woman may contract her own marriage, though her guardian may object to a plainly unsuitable match. Whether a father may marry off a virgin daughter without her word is the oldest dispute here: Hanafis say no, the other three allowed it under conditions, Ibn Taymiyyah rejected it. The Prophet annulled the marriage of a woman whose father had contracted it against her will.

also written Wali · Walee · Waliy · Vali · Veli · Wali nikah

see also

The wedding feast held after the marriage, and a strongly confirmed sunnah on the groom.

The Prophet told 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf to hold one even if only with a single sheep, and he taught that answering the invitation is a duty on those invited unless they have an excuse. Most scholars hold the walimah itself is a confirmed sunnah rather than obligatory. He also warned against a feast to which only the rich are invited and the poor are turned away, which is the part most often forgotten.

also written Walima · Waleema · Valima · Walimat · Walimah urs · Velime

see also

A permanent charitable endowment: property held forever so that its income keeps serving a purpose.

'Umar asked the Prophet about land he had acquired at Khaybar and was told to hold the property itself and give away its produce, which became the model. Once made, a waqf cannot be sold, given away or inherited, and it is administered for its stated beneficiaries, whether a mosque, a school, a well or a family. Historically waqf funded most of the Muslim world's hospitals, libraries and colleges, and it remains the fullest form of ongoing charity.

also written Waqf · Awqaf · Wakf · Vakif · Vakf · Waqaf

see also

Where you stop while reciting, and where you may not, shown by small letters above the line.

The familiar marks come from a system worked out by later scholars rather than from revelation: meem means stop, la means do not stop here, jeem means you may, and paired sets of three dots mean stop at one of the two but not both. Stopping in the wrong place can break the sense of a sentence, which is why the marks were added at all. The same word waqf also means a charitable endowment, an entirely separate subject.

also written Waqaf · Wakf · Waqf signs · Waqf rules · Waqf lazim · Ibtida

see also

Caution that leaves what is unclear, in order to stay safe from what is forbidden.

The Prophet peace be upon him said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters, and whoever avoids them has protected his religion, in Bukhari and Muslim. He also said to leave what makes you uneasy for what does not, in a report collected by Tirmidhi. Wara' works one step further out than taqwa, in the grey band. It becomes a problem only when it turns into suspicion of everything and everyone.

also written Wara · Waraa · War'a · Wara' in food · Scrupulousness · Caution

see also

The reading common in North and West Africa, transmitted by Warsh from Nafi of Madinah.

Uthman ibn Sa'id, nicknamed Warsh, took it from Nafi al-Madani, and it travelled west with the scholars of the Maghrib. Set beside Hafs it lengthens certain vowels further, handles some hamzahs more softly, and tilts some fathas towards a kasra. Nafi's other transmitter is Qalun, whose reading is used in Libya and parts of Tunisia.

also written Warsh · Warsh from Nafi · Warsh an Naafi · Nafi · Naafi · Qalun

see also

A means of nearness to Allah, and also the name of a specific high station in Paradise.

The Qur'an commands: seek the means of nearness to Him (Qur'an 5:35), which the commentators explain as obedience and whatever brings a servant close. The word is also the name of a rank in Paradise which the Prophet peace be upon him said belongs to one servant only, and which he taught his community to ask for on his behalf after the call to prayer. The two meanings share a root and are often mixed up in argument.

also written Waseela · Wasila · Waseelah · Vasila · Al-Wasilah · Means of nearness

see also

A bequest: instructions for up to a third of your estate, taking effect after death.

The Qur'an mentions it before the inheritance shares, and debts are settled before both. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas asked about leaving his whole estate to charity and was told a third, and that even a third is a great deal. A wasiyyah cannot be made in favour of someone who already inherits, since their share is fixed by revelation, so it is used for non heirs, for charity, and for burial and guardianship instructions.

also written Wasiyya · Wasiya · Wasiyat · Wasiyah · Vasiyet · Wasaya

see also

Whispering: unwanted thoughts thrown at the heart, whether by Shaytan or by the mind itself.

The last surah of the Qur'an names the whisperer who whispers in the chests of people (Qur'an 114:4-5). The Prophet peace be upon him said Allah has pardoned this community for what their souls whisper as long as they do not act on it or speak it, in Bukhari and Muslim, and he taught that a person struck by doubts about creation should say I believe in Allah and move on. Distressing repetitive doubt about wudu, prayer or belief is a recognised condition, and treating it as a medical matter as well as a spiritual one is not a failure of faith.

also written Waswas · Waswasa · Wiswas · Waswaas · Wasawis · Khawatir

see also

A personal daily portion of remembrance or recitation that a person keeps to.

The word means a turn at a watering place. In practice a wird is a small fixed amount, a page of Qur'an, a number of salawat, a set of adhkar, repeated every day at the same point. The principle behind it is the prophetic teaching that the deeds most loved by Allah are the constant ones, even if small. Sufi orders assign a specific wird through a shaykh; outside that setting a person simply chooses their own and keeps it.

also written Wirid · Awrad · Wird daily · Daily litany · Litany · Daily portion

see also

An odd-numbered night prayer, usually one or three rak'ahs, that closes the night.

Witr means odd, as opposed to even. It is prayed any time after Isha until dawn, and the Prophet told his companions to make it the last prayer of their night. Hanafis classify it as wajib, close to obligatory; the other three schools call it a confirmed sunnah. Someone who intends to pray tahajjud usually delays witr until after it.

also written Vitr · Vitir · Witir · Wittr · Salatul witr · Witr namaz

see also

The washing done before prayer: face, arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and feet to the ankles.

The four acts are named directly in the Qur'an, and the Prophet added rinsing the mouth and nose, washing the hands first, and doing each part three times. Wudu is broken by using the toilet, by passing wind, and by deep sleep; it is not broken by touching an animal or by ordinary dirt. One wudu lasts for as many prayers as you like until something breaks it.

also written Wudhu · Wuzu · Wazu · Wodu · Wudoo · Abdest

see also

Standing at Arafah on the ninth of Dhul Hijjah, the one rite without which there is no hajj.

The Prophet said the hajj is Arafah. A pilgrim who reaches any part of the plain within its window has performed it, whether standing, sitting or asleep, and one who misses it has missed the hajj that year. The majority date the window from midday until dawn of the next day; Hanbalis start it at dawn on the ninth. The day is spent in supplication rather than in any set ritual.

also written Wuqoof · Wukuf · Wuquf at Arafah · standing at Arafat · Vukuf · Wuquf bi Arafah

see also

Y

Two peoples held back behind a barrier built by Dhu al-Qarnayn, released as a major sign of the Hour.

The Qur'an tells the story of the barrier of iron and molten copper (Qur'an 18:94-98) and says that when they are released they will swarm down from every height (Qur'an 21:96). Scholars have guessed for centuries about who and where they are; the honest answer is that the texts describe a time, not a place on a map. Their release is one of the ten major signs.

also written Yajuj Majuj · Yajooj Majooj · Yajooj wa Majooj · Yaajooj · Gog and Magog · Gog

see also

Certainty: knowledge that has settled to the point where doubt no longer disturbs it.

The Qur'an mentions degrees that scholars read as a ladder: the knowledge of certainty and the eye of certainty (Qur'an 102:5-7), and the truth of certainty (Qur'an 56:95). The difference is like being told about a fire, then seeing it, then feeling its heat. The Qur'an also says worship your Lord until certainty comes to you (Qur'an 15:99), which the commentators explain as death.

also written Yaqeen · Yakin · Yageen · Yaqin billah · Ilm al-yaqin · Ayn al-yaqin

see also

Z

The yearly obligatory share of qualifying wealth, normally 2.5 percent, given to those entitled to it.

The word carries both purification and growth. Zakat is the third pillar, and the Qur'an names it beside the prayer again and again. It is due on savings, gold, silver and trade goods held for a lunar year above the nisab, at one fortieth of their value, while crops, livestock and mined wealth have their own rates. It is a debt owed to specific people, not a donation the giver may direct wherever they wish.

also written Zakah · Zakaat · Zaka · Zekat · Zakat al-mal · Zakaah

see also

A small measure of staple food given for every household member before the Eid al-Fitr prayer.

The Prophet made it obligatory on every Muslim, young and old, free and owned, as a purification for the fasting person and food for the poor. The measure is one sa', roughly two and a half to three kilograms of the local staple. Hanafis permit paying its value in money, which most charities now do; the other schools generally require the food itself. Given after the Eid prayer it counts as ordinary charity, so it is paid early.

also written Zakat ul fitr · Zakatul fitr · Sadaqat al-fitr · Fitrana · Fitrah · Fitra

see also

Zakat on wealth: normally one fortieth of qualifying savings held for a full lunar year.

It is distinguished from zakat al-fitr, the small fixed measure of food given per person at the end of Ramadan. It falls due on cash, gold, silver, trade stock and recoverable debts once they pass the nisab and a lunar year has turned, while crops, livestock and mined wealth have their own rates and no year requirement. Your home, personal belongings and the tools of your trade are exempt. Scholars differ over pensions, shares, and gold jewellery in regular use.

also written Zakat al mal · Zakah al-mal · Zakat ul mal · Zakatul maal · Zakat on wealth · Zakat on savings

see also

The well beside the Ka'bah that opened for Hajar and her infant son Isma'il.

Left in a dry valley with her baby, Hajar ran seven times between two hills looking for help, and water broke open at the child's feet. The name is said to come from her words as she banked the sand to hold it in. The well was lost for centuries and rediscovered by Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet's grandfather. The Prophet said Zamzam water is for whatever it is drunk for, which is why people drink it with an intention rather than out of habit.

also written Zam Zam · Zam-zam · Aab e Zamzam · Ab-e-Zamzam · Water of Zamzam · Zemzem

see also

Sexual intercourse outside marriage: a major sin, and one of the fixed penalty offences.

The Qur'an says do not go near it, calling it an immorality and an evil way, and the wording is read as forbidding the approaches to it as well as the act. The penalty carries a bar of proof so high it is almost never reached, four upright witnesses to the act itself, and the same passage punishes those who make the accusation without them. Islamic law discourages prying, and consistently prefers concealment and repentance to exposure.

also written Zinaa · Zena · Zinah · Zani · Zaniyah · Zina bil jabr

see also

Holding the world loosely: having a thing in your hand without letting it into your heart.

The Prophet peace be upon him told a man to be indifferent to the world and Allah would love him, and to be indifferent to what people own and people would love him, in a report collected by Ibn Majah. Scholars are clear that zuhd is not poverty and not refusing what is lawful; several Companions were wealthy. It is the willingness to lose a thing without losing yourself along with it.

also written Zuhud · Zohd · Zuhd fid dunya · Zahid · Asceticism · Detachment
